utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Mr. Tieger, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And good morning to all in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, as we began before we adjourned yesterday, I want to draw your attention and the Court's attention to D03019, the letter you sent on 18 December 1995 to Mr. Lavrov. Now, first of all, let's confirm a few details. You have indicated in your statement at paragraph 71 that the letter was sent inadvertently to the Security Council instead of Lavrov, so you mentioned him in your statement. Mr. Lavrov at the time was the president of the Security Council, correct, in addition to being head of the Russian mission?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were two letters. One was the letter, or rather, the report from the president of the municipality of Srebrenica and the other is the letter you referred to, namely the letter addressed to Ambassador Lavrov, as chairman of the Security Council. I think these are two different matters, because in this letter which is shorter, just a page and a half or so, there are certain allusions to the Srebrenica case but not in so much detail as the letter that I received from the president of Srebrenica municipality --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Jovanovic --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so that the letter --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- the letter is in front of you right now. Let's turn to the next page so the witness can see it, please. This is D3019, which was appended to your statement and admitted to this Court. So that's the letter we're talking about; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the letters. This letter was correctly addressed to the president of the Security Council and the other letter was supposed to be sent to Lavrov, but by mistake also went to the Security Council and that created both confusion and dissatisfaction at the Security Council. It is my mistake that it ended up in the Security Council instead of just in the hands of Mr. Lavrov as chairman of the Russian delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, what you purposely sent to Mr. Lavrov, as we see on the screen before you --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- states in part, as we turn to the next page, that before the forces of Republika Srpska entered Srebrenica there was merciless killing within the Bosnian army and, in essence, states that the Muslim victims were responsible for their own deaths; correct? That is what you submitted to Mr. Lavrov.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I should like to be more precise here because this is a longer text than the one I had in mind. This text was supposed to go only to Lavrov as Russia's permanent representative at the United Nations. But my mistake it was addressed to Lavrov as head of the Security Council, and that caused confusion and my personal dissatisfaction over that faux pas, but that was only my mistake and nobody else's.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This was submitted in anticipation of a Security Council session that would be dedicated to the issue of Srebrenica; correct? And that's what you testified to in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that was the day before the meeting of the Security Council that this letter was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to look at some of the things -- some of the things you have said about Srebrenica and ask you if you confirm or deny those things. You testified in the Milosevic case in 2005 that with regard -- well: "If you're referring to Srebrenica in 1995, then that was an atrocious massacre." That's at 36333 through 34; correct? You stated that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that is still my opinion today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And you were interviewed by a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor in 2009 in April and you stated at that time that Srebrenica was a massive massacre, not acceptable at all; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You stated that it was very sad: "Very sad that Serbs were involved in that kind of crime. It's -- it's terrible. Once this prisoner or enemy he should be respected. It has always been the custom of Serbian armed forces throughout the history so it was very bad thing which happened there." Correct? That's what you told the Office -- the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor in 2009.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then when asked who was responsible, you stated: "Those who made such a crime - and I don't know whether they did it with the knowledge of their superiors or not ..." And when asked who "they" were, that is, the superiors, you stated "Mladic and Karadzic." And that's also what you stated to the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor in 2009; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct insofar as both President Karadzic and General Mladic were two personalities at the top of Republika Srpska, one in the military, one in the political sense. But that doesn't mean that those who committed those crimes received their approval to commit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also gave an interview to "Slobodna Bosna" in 2008, that is, in November 2008, and that's 65 ter 24669, if we can call that up. It may be under 24669A. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm told that the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- hasn't been released yet. 24669A.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a portion of that interview, sir. It begins with your comments about Sarajevo, indicating you could not understand about Sarajevo at all, why keep a city under siege for so long, for three and a half years, why subject it to all those snipers and misfortunes? You go on to indicate that you did ask Karadzic a few times, explained that this was causing a great deal of damage to their legitimate goals and to us all. And then you follow with his -- what he said, that the enemy must be prevented from having free hands and from free actions. And then you stated: "As far as Srebrenica is concerned, that was a dreadful crime, unjustified. It cannot be justified by any ... even if just a single captured soldier was executed - the crime was dreadful, but so many of them - even it is not 8.000 but 1.000, 2.000, 3.000, or 4.000 - that is a dreadful crime that does not diminish this. I just think that all those who are responsible for those crimes as well as for all the others, the criminals, should be held responsible." And that is also a reflection of the positions that you've taken over the years about Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but that does not still reveal the full truth about who in addition to Serbs, if there were any or others, was involved in those crimes because that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- side of it has not been shed any light on yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about what you stated and that's the -- I'm not asking -- I'm not entering into a debate with you about all the details of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender 24669A.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President. But I would just note that when Mr. Tieger asked a question such as that which he did, that still does not reveal the truth about who ... you know: This is a reflection of the positions that you've taken over the years about Srebrenica; correct? I think the witness should be given a chance to explain his views about Srebrenica when a question like that is asked and I think Mr. Tieger was wrong to cut the witness off and expect some kind of yes or no answer to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, I think the witness has answered the question. And if necessary, Mr. Karadzic may take up that issue in his re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. -- thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you need more -- do you still have further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just following up on this, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll give the number for that document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6150, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, when you submitted your letter to Mr. Lavrov in December of 1995, you didn't indicate to him any of the views or information contained in the excerpts that I've just drawn your attention to; that is, you didn't indicate to him what you've told the Milosevic Trial Chamber, what you said in 2009 to the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, or what you told the interviewer from "Slobodna Bosna," did you?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letter that I sent, or rather, that my deputy was supposed to send to Ambassador Lavrov contains some of the points from the report of the president of Srebrenica municipality, and this paper was supposed to be useful to Ambassador Lavrov in his speech to the Security Council. My objective was not to share my opinion with him, nor was my opinion then sufficient, nor was I in the know about all the details of the atrocity committed there. I just sent that paper without going into which part of that was true or not. At that time, I did not even have a full opinion. I did not have enough information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And now, nearly 20 years later, you draw the Trial Chamber's -- this Trial Chamber's attention to that same report, a report which alleges that the victims of Srebrenica killed themselves, and you don't provide any information to the Trial Chamber whatsoever in your statement about what you said to the Trial Chamber in Milosevic in 2005, about what you said to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2009, about what you said to "Slobodna Bosna" in 2008 about the fact that you consider that it was the forces of Republika Srpska that executed unarmed prisoners. That's the fact, isn't it, sir? There's nothing of that in your statement, is there?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not in my statement because the only two weeks before Mustafic, a representative of the political bodies of Bosnian Muslims, had given a statement where he claimed --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that Bosnian Muslims under Naser Oric -- please allow me to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's hear him out and then ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That Naser Oric is directly responsible for the death of 500 to 1.000 Bosnian Muslims from Srebrenica, and that allegedly that number of Muslim soldiers were executed on their way from Srebrenica to Tuzla. That is the claim of that man and that can be easily checked because he is one of the more prominent Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina who deals with this subject in a expert way. Certain details about the full truth of what happened in Srebrenica came only later, subsequently. And then on the 18th December 2005, I was not in a position to find out anything more than I could read from the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellency, Mr. Jovanovic. I'll start with the freshest point: Did my Defence team ask you about your knowledge from 1995 or from 2005 or now 2013 regarding Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, they asked me what I knew at that time when it was all happening, in 2005 [sic]. The knowledge I gained later, like everybody else, is a combination of what I learned from various sides and could or could not be relevant. But it is certainly not the same as what I knew in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I take it you meant 1995, not 2005?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I misspoke. I meant 1995. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked a short time ago whether you shared with the Defence team the knowledge you gained later subsequently. Has there been an investigation that you'd had access to regarding events in Srebrenica so that you would have been able to gain that knowledge at the time of the interview?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like everyone else in the past 15, 20 years, I tried to read more and find out more, both from the work of this Tribunal and the work of others and provided contributions based on fact or facts that were not completely consistent with what this Court has found in its various judgements. But I still do not have a precise enough picture about how many of those unfortunate people were killed there. I have the impression that it is overblown and exaggerated, and it's not clear whether only those local Serbs were to blame or perhaps part of the blame lies on the Bosnian Muslims, as Mr. Mustafic claimed recently. I cannot completely trust anyone. I can only read and listen and try to make my own judgement, and that judgement is not definitive yet, especially if we compare the massacre in Srebrenica with the massacre in the Katin forest where 22.000 officers and soldiers were killed. And nobody has been charged for that crime yet, not Stalin and not Russia have been charged for the crime, only the massacre. That is what makes me still hesitant to make a final qualification of that crime. Nobody in Russia has been charged with genocide.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 11, the word "genocide" was omitted -- now it has been corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, regarding that letter dated 18 December 1995, did you or your government try or did you gain the impression that my government was trying to conceal anything regarding the events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I requested information as soon as Lavrov requested it from me because I had no contacts whatsoever, and several times I insisted and for a long time I did not receive that answer. But I finally received the answer in the form of a copy of the report from the president of Srebrenica municipality, and that reply was several times longer than the letter I eventually sent there. Because not all the elements contained in the Srebrenica report seemed relevant to me for the debate the Security Council and Ambassador Lavrov. I asked my deputy to excerpt those points that were the most relevant and he did that and I signed it by mistake. So that was the result. I glanced through the report very quickly because I didn't have much time. This needed to be sent very quickly. The meeting of the Security Council was already scheduled for the next day. But I could see that it was made up of elements that were not very coherent and did not look very convincing at first glance. As far as the leadership of Republika Srpska is concerned, my impression was that they were not involved, that they did not know about that letter, and that President wrote it alone. Nobody but him was in a position to provide a more global view of the events in that area at the time so that if Republika Srpska had been in the know, I suppose that they would have sent some sort of report themselves. However, we didn't receive any reports from them, only from the president of the municipality of Srebrenica. And as I later found out, the leadership of Republika Srpska was not aware of that report. I don't know if they still are. It seemed to me just a report from the local level, not what I requested.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see that letter again in e-court, D3019.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, did you plead that what you conveyed from that letter be taken for granted or be subjected to further inquiry?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean my letter to Lavrov? At that point I was not in a position to assess the significance or the accuracy of what we received from Srebrenica. And that's why we forwarded it all, I mean the usable part, to Lavrov for him to judge for himself whether there was anything useful in that or not. However, through my mistake it was made available to all members of the Security Council and created confusion. I really had no precise idea of what had happened there really. During my tenure as a minister, telegrams arrived from --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, I'm only interested in this letter. Could we see the last page. Let us see if this is accurate. Item 4, the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. "In view of the foregoing ..." was that your position, that an investigation needed to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. The Security Council session was also aimed at finding out what was going on. You cannot find out everything at a single meeting. There have to be several -- there has to be more information about what happened there. So that meeting was just supposed to be the beginning of an investigation that would lead to the full truth. I do not remember exactly whether the meeting of the Security Council acted that way or whether they condemned the crime in Srebrenica immediately, taking a position that basically remained unchanged throughout. I don't remember whether it happened then already or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Excellency, I don't need to tender this, but could the usher please show on the ELMO a few recent clips from the media where official representatives of the Muslims of Srebrenica are speaking about what you found strange in that letter of the president of the municipality of Srebrenica. So I just really want to ask you whether that's that.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise, but what is it that you actually mean by this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What you said a moment ago, what this -- what one of them stated now and -- I mean it was Ibran Mustafic.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yes, Ibran Mustafic was the last one and before that there was this other historian, Mehulic, Mihulic, a Muslim. He claimed -- he presented the assertion that in 1993 President Clinton proposed to the late Izetbegovic that they provoked the Serbs around Srebrenica so that 5.000 Muslims would go missing and that would suffice for NATO intervention. He claims in that book - and no one's denied it yet, I don't know to what extent this is true or not. But Mustafic repeated that idea in relation to 1995 and he claimed something that I found hard to believe in 1995. However, when he asserted now that Naser Oric was directly responsible for the death of 500 to 1.000 Muslim soldiers, which was later ascribed to the Serbs as a crime of theirs, then a person has to remain confused, wondering what is true, like Pontius Pilot almost. I personally would like to find out the entire truth, not only part of the truth, regardless of whether it is pleasant or not. And I think it is in everybody's interest to find out the truth. Now information is coming from other sides as well, indicating that the full truth regarding Srebrenica has not been established yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just show the first pages with the headings so that we will see whether that is what you meant when you spoke of recent news.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's in B/C/S. I presume it's meant to be some kind of confirmation of or reflection of what the witness was referring to, but in my submission I don't -- he can show it on the ELMO if he wants, if that is what it purports to be. But the issue really is what this witness purported to know at any given time. So any document that strays beyond that is obviously inappropriate. But this is a direct reference to what the witness was talking about. I don't have any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I was about to ask you and Mr. Karadzic whether we had that part of evidence in our evidence already, i.e., Mustafic's claim or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it's a general matter. We do. I understand this to be a kind of direct follow-up to what the witness just said, that is -- and it could have been done in the way the Court just indicated. It appears it's being done in a slightly different manner, but I think it's at this moment restricted to that so I don't object to that. But in terms of expedition, we could just -- if he -- if Dr. Karadzic could cite the previous evidence, that would suffice also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's proceed. Is the ELMO working? No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I can ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, what was unusual and unconvincing? What was it that made you uncomfortable with regard to that letter of the president of the municipality of Srebrenica, that Serb?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but the first thing that led to my confusion was that at the very beginning of the letter he claimed that the Muslims in Srebrenica killed each other. There were some who wanted to stay on and fight and others who did not want to do that. So allegedly those who wanted to fight fired at those who did not want to. That seemed somehow unconvincing to me, and I simply could not take it that way until only a couple of weeks ago when I heard Mustafic, what he had to say, and then I remembered that dilemma of mine and then it became even deeper; namely, it seemed that that kind of thing had been possible after all. Now, whether it was to the extent that has been suggested or not, that I cannot judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency. Could we please display now what we have from the media, the second half of February, only recently, two weeks ago. So does that cast a bit more light on what it was that you held against that report at the time, what made you uncomfortable, and what you found strange in that report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At the moment, the ELMO doesn't seem to be functioning. How many photocopies do you have with you now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One each, Excellency, but copies can be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have other topics to deal with? A technician is on his way to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one more question in relation to that letter of the 18th of December. Excellency, was the wish of your government granted, that is to say to have this investigation carried out? Was an investigation ever carried out that would lead to full evidence in terms of what had happened there?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in New York at the time. I don't know about all the things that the government in Belgrade was doing on that score; however, I do know - and I repeated that beforehand - that Milosevic insisted all the time that the safe zones do not be touched, do not be attacked, and some kind of danger of that kind was looming. Now, our authorities in Belgrade, to what extent they asked for a full investigation to be carried out, I don't know. Probably there were some initiatives, some requests, but I cannot assert anything in this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 34304 it was stated to you that at a session held on the 9th of January, 1993 -- that is 65 ter 06145 on page 68 in English and 67 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sixty-eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It has to do with the topic of Greater Serbia, and it was stated what I said: [In English] "It is a long-term aim which could be achieved only step by step or gradually." [Interpretation] I would like to show you the part that had not been quoted to you. Do you remember that? 65 ter 6145, could we have that, please. Page 12 in both Serbian and English and then page 13. So this is where Karadzic's remarks start and -- ah, yes, please. I recall the Atlantic Charter here, the USA and the UK and this is what it says: "These states respect the rights of all nations to choose the form of government under which they wish to live. Sovereign rights and the rights of governing themselves should be returned to those from whom they had been taken by force. That is to say that they do not wish to deprive us of our rights by force. They are asking for our co-operation in our own destruction." And then it says: "All our attempts to make a compromising -- a document that would be based on compromise were rejected ..." And then further on it says: "All our attempts to open the door in terms of terminology that this would be a community of nations, even a unitary state or even a single unitary state gives us the -- all of that was rejected and avoided." Excellency, is this in line with your own understanding of our position about the nature of our staying in Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was it that we had asked for and that we had been deprived of?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully understand that and I don't think it is difficult to draw a conclusion on the basis of all of this, that your objective was that within Bosnia there be a very loose relationship between and among the three peoples, that this be some kind of confederacy union or whatever. This is something that the Croat side accepted but the Muslim side did not want to accept that at any cost. They wanted a unitary Bosnia. The international mediators did not deal with that question at that level, as you had requested. All the way up until June or July 1993 when Owen for the first time came up with the idea of this union of Bosnia, a confederation in Bosnia, it was only then that this idea grew its roots, eventually growing into a tree that ended in the Dayton Accords. This has nothing to do with the Greater Serbia. It would have something to do with the Greater Serbia had you been fighting for annexing that part of Bosnia that you populate to Serbia. But that's not what you wanted to do. Your first objective was to be loyal to the common state and not to leave that common state. That was a natural and legitimate right of all who lived in the country, to be loyal to that country. When that was no longer possible after the international recognition of Bosnia, your objectives were related to the framework of that state, Bosnia. But you went much further and the Muslim side did not even want to accept that as a topic for discussion, let alone to agree to it all together. All the way up to mid-1993, this idea of an ethnically regulated union according to an ethnic principle, that was not being bandied about, but then it became stronger and to this day it is there. This idea of a Greater Serbia which was un -- which was untrue from the very beginning, and I think that the Court was even misled into thinking that. What does a Greater Serbia mean? Is it something that is in the mind of certain people or is it a project that exists? There never was such a project and there isn't one now. What is Risorgimento? What is the unification of Germany? What is the megalo-idea of Germany? All of them have the idea of national unification. I am sorry. So all of these states that were not put together, I mean their peoples were not put together, they all have this dream, they even have these projects to live all together in one state. That, in itself, is not a reason for condemning them. Why would the Serb people be apart from all others and why would they be stigmatised in a negative sense just because they also have this natural aspiration to live in a single state? Even more so because all Serbs had already lived in a single state, the socialist Yugoslavia; that was broken up and they were forcibly taken out of that state. So this part about a Greater Serbia, this idea of a Greater Serbia was abandoned by this court also, rightly so I believe, and I think that there is no point in bringing it up again because this is not part of political or national reality of any of the Serbs living in the Balkans today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency. Now we get to the question that was raised by Mr. Tieger as well in relation to dreams, no matter how legitimate or illegitimate they may be. Did you see for yourself that I was prepared to sacrifice peace for any idea or any dream? Did you ever see anything like that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are a poet, first and foremost, and you let your imagination go and then people who have been deprived of that kind of gift cannot understand that. It is a fact that you never wrote any such thing or uttered any such thing that for obtaining your political objective you were prepared to sacrifice peace. You never stated that. You never worked in that direction; however, others did. The late Alija Izetbegovic said that quite openly, and on the other side Tudjman said that too. After all, in the eastern declaration, that is the alpha and the omega, that is the doctrine of the Bosnian Muslims, and it is explicitly stated that there is no peace between the fateful and the unfaithful, the Muslims and the infidels. After that Alija Izetbegovic did not want to discuss that but, after all, that is his Bible, the Islamic Declaration. When the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina heard about that and they were such victims during the Second World War, of course it made their hairs stand on end, and of course they didn't want to be in that situation again. So this Bosnian situation, this Bosnian caldron, consisting of various rational and irrational elements, it is hard, it is perhaps irresponsible to simplify this in terms of one side only or the guilt of one side only. Simply, this is not a path that leads to the truth, but this is a path that leads us astray, away from the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we see page 27 of this document, please. You were quoted back your words, but not in their entirety or not to a sufficient degree. What was quoted to you was on transcript page 34304, and now I would like to show you the part where you allegedly said that the international community and the conditions do not permit for the dreams to come true, the dreams on Serbian state, Serbian country. In the first paragraph it says: "We had heard from Mr. Karadzic that Americans called parts of their country states the same as done by Switzerland and Germany and many other countries. How come they do not want the word 'state' to be the word which would denote the unified Serbian ethnical territory in Bosnia? It is obvious that they have some ulterior motives and by eliminating that word they want to predetermine the future self-determination of Serbs in Bosnia. If they give up on that now, in the future they would not be able to invoke that. So this fear from the change of our constitutional status" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the point of question, Mr. -- just ask the question. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, that's exactly right and it's very clear a leading question is about to unfold.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I just wanted to quote fully what Minister Jovanovic stated at the time. It wasn't quoted in its entirety on the page that I quoted from the transcript. And I wanted to hear from His Excellency whether this was a more complete quotation of his words and whether that truly reflected his position at the time and our views on that subject.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is the condensed version of the reality in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time and the greatest fears of the Serbs in Bosnia at the time. They did not want to be pushed out as the constituent nation. They didn't want to be sucked into some kind of a unitary state. And this fear of theirs had its historical basis, and occasionally it may have received some irrational forms in these poetical moments, but in reality it was realistically grounded. The Bosnian Muslims did not want to remain in the Socialist Yugoslavia any longer, and the Serbs in Bosnia were wondering whether they could remain in Bosnia which was a miniature version of Yugoslavia itself. So I'm coming back to what I said earlier, that the destruction of the Socialist Yugoslavia was a crime which pushed the situation into a series of new crimes which continued to this day. The responsibility of those who had destroyed Yugoslavia has not been evaluated in court yet. No investigation was launched against those who initiated this destruction of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What the Prosecutor did not quote to you, speaking about the unitary state, I will quote now. Perhaps in parallel with that insistence and with those explanations, legal, political, and moral, we should also offer guarantees that such statehood within Bosnia does not in any way represent an expansion of Serbia towards Bosnia nor does it represent the creation of the Greater Serbia, nor does it create basis for future or indirect secession of that Serbian state from Bosnia. This could be achieved by providing guarantees, international, ours, and Croatian. How does this relate to allegations that there were stories about joining up Serbian expansionism?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those stories were constantly planted by Bosnian Muslims to the international community in order to scare, to create fear, in the international community of this monster called Serbia who couldn't wait to swallow up smaller countries around it. This was their platform for leaving Yugoslavia and creating their independent states, falsely representing the situation as a danger of them being swallowed up by Serbia. Because had this -- or argument really been solid, then the same danger would have existed for Croats and Bosnian Serbs of them being swallowed up by Bosnian Muslims. So that was not the valid logic. The proper way was to establish proper relations within a multi-ethnic state, not to stir up these fears. What I explained here is nothing new. The state entity within Bosnia and Herzegovina was something that would have calmed down the fears of both Serbs and Croats in Bosnia, their fear of Muslims, and would have prevent the Muslim from carrying out the unitarisation by force. So the problems that we mentioned concerning Bavaria in Germany and various cantons in Switzerland and the republics in Yugoslavia which were organised as states within the country. All of that was not a sufficient reason for the international community to scream around that that was the way to disintegrate a state. The Dayton Agreement confirmed these two state entities within Bosnia and Herzegovina and that was a precondition for a peaceful coexistence and further continuation of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Excellency. On page 34318 it was suggested to you that you spoke about ethnic homogeneity and the ethnical principle as a strategic objective. Not everything was quoted back to you, not all of your words were quoted back to you as you uttered them at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see P794, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So in that question it was suggested to you that you supported the idea of them being founded on an ethnic principle, of them being ethnic cantons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 5, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at the second paragraph, Your Excellency. You say there: "It would be bad if we insisted on the national, it needs to come on its own ..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it's page 5 in the English as well -- no, page 4 in the English version, second paragraph in the address by Minister Jovanovic beginning with the words "it would be ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "It should simply happen naturally, on its own, because they have already accepted it. We should insist on the economic principle and use it to improve the territorial appearance of things, while the national principle should be insisted upon only to the extent which is needed for providing life-lines, in other words, to link it with the zones within the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This holds. This holds to this day. I see things the same way nowadays too. Muslims and Croats had already opted for the national principle in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in the name of that national principle they had seceded. They left Yugoslavia. So why would that national principle be denied only to the Serbs in Bosnia? Because all of those three communities in a kind of way had their own territories, and unfortunately that was also the result of the war, the consequence of the war. But even prior to that they started creating their own territories on the national basis. For me, much more important than the national principle was the economic sustainability because that was the precondition for everything, and I kept warning them that they shouldn't be obsessed with the national principle but should rather worry about what is in the source of life which was the economic principle. It was important for the Serbs in Bosnia to be a direct contact, to be able to lean on Serbia in order to continue the co-operation, cultural, economic, spiritual co-operation between two parts of the same nation. And this is something that the Contact Group had already enabled the Bosnian Croats to have with the Croats in Croatia. And Dayton later enabled that to the Serbs in Bosnia to have those kind of ties with Serbia, and so I stand by these words now as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your interview given to "Slobodna Bosna" you said that I had said that in a war one should prevent the enemy from doing what they wanted. Did you know, Excellency, that in Sarajevo there were armed formations and armed forces of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina or was it some kind of an urban --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, I mean I think that's ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the interpretation. [In English] Whether you knew about what was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it -- I think Dr. Karadzic can try as hard as he wants to polish this question, but it remains a leading question even as he tries to tinker with the precise formulation. He's providing -- he's directing the witness's attention to aspects of the answer that he ultimately seeks.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to reformulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, did you know that or were there in Sarajevo any enemy forces whom we should have kept tied, whose hands we should have kept tied?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ask a question of relevance. I mean, the issue is -- begins with what was related to him by the accused, which doesn't open the door to an explanation of the -- what the witness may or may not consider to be the overall rationale or justification behind any actions taken by the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the witness was not there. Consider how much value, probative value, it will have. Let's proceed. Move -- please move on. The document is on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I now ask you to look at the date, please, on this internet announcement -- this text that appeared on the internet, could you now tell us what it is about?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a statement or a book by Mr. Mustafic. We created a sensation a couple of weeks ago, if I remember well, stating that Naser Oric was directly responsible for the death of 500 to 1.000 Bosniaks from Srebrenica whom he killed on as they travelled from Srebrenica to Tuzla. Apparently he had been dissatisfied with them because they did not want to remain and continue defending Srebrenica, but I will not go into that. I would like to remind you also of another instance which was recently uncovered, namely, the killing of the two young people on the demarcation line between the Muslim and the Serbian part of Sarajevo. It was then discovered, it was discovered just now, that they had been killed by Muslim sniper and that it was attributed to the Serbs. That was a young couple, a Serb and a young Muslim woman, who had been killed. So these things are coming out now and perhaps they cannot give you the entire picture, but they definitely show that there are things that were suppressed, that we didn't know about, and that nobody wanted to discuss. For me, these are revelations, revelations that confuse me because all of a sudden I see that this assertion that the Muslims killed each other is less likely than -- less improbable [Realtime transcript read in error "probable"] than I had thought 15 or 18 years ago. There was a young Muslim woman who came to me and who spoke to me openly, and she was -- she interviewed me and she was supposed to send me the text later on to authorise it. She didn't do it properly. She obviously wanted to adapt that text to the needs, to the political needs, of the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In line 12 it should say "less unbelievable," not "less probable." "Less improbable," that's how it should be. The witness said that it is now less improbable than it had seemed to him 18 years ago.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now put the cover pages of these additional two documents, please, on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I object to that. The witness is -- the Court is aware of why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will retract this. We will give up on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You asked on page 73 yesterday -- you were asked on page 73 yesterday -- or rather, on page 93 you were asked about the ethnic cleansing. Excellency, Your Excellency, were you familiar with our position on the right to return and was this -- did we ever challenge that right to return?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that was your position and when I once conveyed the objections of international mediators, stating that in the Republika Srpska organs there had not been sufficient representation by Serbs and Muslims in Bosnia -- by Croats and Muslims in Bosnia, you in response said that there were a lot of them in the army. And that was your official position which I remembered as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Excellency. I have no further questions, some minor ones which are not that important. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With the Court's leave could I address just one issue that arose twice that can be clarified, I trust, quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With respect to that internet clipping?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With -- well, with respect to that -- to that issue that was raised, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Further cross-examination by Mr. Tieger:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, there's been some discussion during the re-direct examination about information that you received two weeks ago in relation to your statement. Now, is it correct, sir, that you signed your statement on February 20 -- your final statement on February 22nd of this year, you just recently signed it?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It signed it. I don't remember which date it was, but I did sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you made certain limited modifications to an earlier statement that you had provided to the Defence; correct? So the statement you signed was the -- was a reflection of the earlier statement you had given the Defence with certain corrections or additions that made -- made this month?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What exactly do you have in mind? I can't reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The statement that you signed was not created completely on the date you signed it. You came here for proofing, you made certain modifications to a statement you had given much earlier, and then you signed that; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think those were minor changes, minor modifications, that did not affect the essence of the matters that I discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the earlier statement was given sometime last year, correct, or even earlier?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the statement that I signed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I mean the statement that you looked at and made corrections to this month. That statement was given last year or earlier; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably at the end of last year. I don't remember exactly. On the other hand, I don't see why I shouldn't have made modifications or given additional clarifications. All of that is part of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the only modification you made to paragraph 71 was to indicate that Ambassador -- that you prepared a letter for Ambassador Lavrov and you added "in his capacity as the Russian representative to the Security Council and not in his capacity of the Presidency of the Security Council." Correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was convinced that the letter was addressed to Ambassador Lavrov as the Russian representative at the UN, and as I have explained --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, you don't have to --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it was sent --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have explained it and I just wanted to note the chronology. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's all I have, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless my colleagues have questions for you, Mr. Jovanovic, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I take it the next witness is Mr. Lelek?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. He's ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was -- this system is slow today so I wanted to be completely logged off so Ms. Gustafson will take the next witness. It could make the transition quickly. I still think that will be possible, so I'm not seeking a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lelek. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Lelek, I must draw your attention to a certain Rule of Procedure and Evidence that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). Under this Rule you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lelek. Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Lelek.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask you and remind myself to make pauses between questions and answers and speak more slowly so that everything would be recorded properly and interpreted correctly. Could we see in e-court 1D7812. Please look at the screen. Can you see your statement on the display?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed that statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I have read it and signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement accurately reflect what you stated to the Defence team in your answers to their questions?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put to you here in the courtroom the same questions, would your answers be essentially the same?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Essentially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, may I tender this 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we're tendering five associated exhibits and for each of them we ask permission to add them to our 65 ter list, as we hadn't interviewed this witness at the time that list was filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: To the exhibits, Your Honour, no. Except I note that 1D06837 referenced at paragraph 24 has been admitted as P4769. And we do have a partial objection to the admission of the statement. We had communicated that in general terms on Monday. It was the additional seven paragraphs added to the end of the statement that in our submission go beyond the minor changes permitted to be made at the 48-hour stage. There are seven new paragraphs on new topics going to the core of the case in this municipality that weren't raised before in the statement. So I believe this is outside the minor changes or corrections provided in the Chamber's earlier guidance. In addition, although that's reason enough alone for those paragraphs to be led live, I note that the manner in which the information in these paragraphs was elicited was done by way of putting a series of adjudicated facts to the witness and asking for his comments. Those comments have then been provided in a -- rather conclusory assertive terms, and there is no foundation provided for the witness's purported knowledge and none is apparent from the rest of the statement. So that, in my submission, is another reason for this information to be led live; otherwise, in cross-examination I will be required to first elicit the foundation for these claims that should have been elicited in the statement or in direct before I'm able to confront them which causes two problems. First, a time issue because I just simply don't have the time to do and that; and, secondly, a notice issue because I'll have to spontaneously respond to the witness's answers. And I don't think that's fair in the circumstances, given that this is really something that should be elicited by the party calling the witness. So for those two reasons together, these paragraphs, in our submission, should be led live. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To confirm, those seven paragraphs are paras from 26 to the end?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to respond, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think there's a number of misconceptions that underline this objection. The first is that we would only be entitled to make minor adjustments to the statement. I think that -- while we do try to make the adjustments to the statement as unobtrusive as possible so that the trial can proceed without delay or interruption, Dr. Karadzic is representing himself, he's in custody, and he doesn't have the same freedom that the Prosecution has to obtain the information from its witnesses at an earlier stage. So in order to effect that right, sometimes he -- we have to add information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He could be represented then if it obstructs his Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well then the right to self-representation wouldn't exist at this Tribunal. And this Appeals Chamber has said clearly that it does exist, that it's a right that goes back to many international instruments and not only the Statute but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. So if I could also indicate that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But what we referred to was one of notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Exactly, which is what my next point is, and that is the remedy for notice. When the Prosecution is disadvantaged by late notice of additional material, we're always willing to postpone the testimony of the witness or the cross-examination so that they can have enough time to adjust. And we're happy to do that even at this stage, to call the next witness in, give Ms. Gustafson as much time as she thinks she needs to adjust to this information. And finally with respect to her point that there's inadequate foundation for the material in the statement: First of all, I do agree that it would be much better if we had actually set forth the adjudicated fact in the statement so that the Chamber can see exactly what the witness was referring to, and we're going to do that in the future. But nevertheless, Rule 92 ter statements are not objectionable because they haven't been -- the witness's position isn't explained in enough detail. The remedy for that is for the Prosecution to ask the witness questions about that, not to tell us how to reformulate the statement. And we didn't ask the Prosecutor to reformulate their Rule 92 ter statements. And again, if Ms. Gustafson needs more time than the Chamber allotted for her cross-examination in which to do that, then she could have that. But leading live is a remedy that's incongruous to the situation. It just wastes the Chamber's time and it has no benefit to the Prosecution or to the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably I have to ask you again, Mr. Robinson, what prejudice would there be if the accused is to be ordered to lead live some part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: None at all, Mr. President, so long as you add the hours or don't subtract that time from the hours. So any time you would like to hear something live, we're happy to do that, so long as it doesn't prevent us from calling other witnesses by reducing the time that we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Maybe I can just clear up a misconception, and I apologise if I was unclear. The foundation issue wasn't that the adjudicated facts were just stated by number. I just note that that's a somewhat odd way to proceed when a witness hasn't provided any information about an event to put to him Prosecution evidence and ask him for his comment and the result in this case has been these sweeping assertions negating those -- negating that evidence without any apparent foundation or certainly none that was provided. So I just noted the way the evidence was elicited. It didn't seem to me to be something for which there was any real forensic need to elicit the evidence in this way. And it is a rather more leading and suggestive way to get the witness's evidence. But it's really the result of that that caused me concern. So I just wanted to clear that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the time, the Chamber will have a break now for half an hour and resume at 11.00. We'll give a ruling when we resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, just very quickly, it occurred to me that I should perhaps make explicit of what is essentially implicit through our practice, and that is that I will be providing to Mr. Robinson, and we've discussed this in relationship to the last witnesses even before his testimony concluded, the excerpts referred to during the testimony, at least those that were not confirmed by the witness to see if there is any dispute about which ones those represent and then tendering those for admission. I had discussed that with Mr. Robinson I think even before the witness's -- the witness examination began, but I failed to state it specifically when his evidence concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We'll look at that and try to come to some agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll now issue an oral ruling on the Prosecution's partial objection to the admission of Mr. Lelek's witness statement in light of the late addition of seven paragraphs to the statement. The Chamber recalls its practice exercised during both the Prosecution and Defence case to order that a witness be led live regarding evidence that is added within 48 hours to a witness's Rule 92 ter statement and thus does not provide appropriate notice to the opposing party. In the present case the Chamber considers that the seven paragraphs added to Mr. Lelek's statement constitute a significant enough amendment to provide inadequate notice to the Prosecution and thus orders that these portions be led live. In addition, as regards one of the associated exhibits, i.e., 1D6833, while the statement suggests that this document confirms "lies and fabrication" with respect to Bosnian Serbs, it's not clear how this document demonstrates this. So I would like the accused to lead live if he's minded to tender this document. That said, we'll admit the Rule 92 ter statement as well as the other -- the three remaining associated exhibits, i.e., from 6834 to 6836.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, they will be admitted as Exhibits D3031 through D3034 respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read the summary of Mr. Milovan Lelek's statement in English. [In English] As a reserve army officer, Mr. Milovan Lelek was assistant commander of the Rogatica Territorial Defence prior to war -- to the war. After the outbreak of the war, he became Chief of Staff of the Rogatica 1st Light Infantry Brigade. Mr. Milovan Lelek noted that Muslims erected barricades in the villages in March 1992, and at this time the political and security situation in Rogatica was becoming increasingly more complex. He was informed that the situation in the town was very bad and that ethnic relations had totally deteriorated. There were preparations to divide the municipality into Serbian and Muslim areas and the Territorial Defence be split up. He was also informed that the Muslims were creating paramilitary units. A Serb Territorial Defence had been formed to protect the local Serbian villages; however, there were only about 20 people and were mostly armed with their own weapons. Milovan Lelek was called up towards the end of May 1992, and when he was stationed in Borike he noticed that the unit frequently came under attack from all kinds of modern infantry weapons which also occurred during the cease-fire period. The Serb forces respected the periods of cease-fire, and if they came under fire in this period they sought permission to return fire. The unit listened to the Radio BH which broadcasted the reports from Fadil Heljic about the Muslims being shelled by Chetniks, freezing and starving to death. Milovan Lelek is aware that Fadil Heljic received orders to bombard the public with such statements and further that he was ordered to dig graves by the sides of the road used by the humanitarian convoys to imply that more people were being killed than they actually were, presenting the Muslims as martyrs. The killing of Drazenko Mihajlovic marked the beginning of war in Rogatica, when Muslim forces would not allow his body to be recovered. Communications with other units and higher commands were maintained around Rogatica throughout the fighting and daily combat reports were sent. The lines of defence established at the beginning of the fighting were held until the end of the war. During the fighting, terrorist groups often killed local civilians and mined the roads around. When the VRS was formed, the Territorial Defence was reformed, the unit of which Milovan Lelek was a member, was manned only by personnel from the area of Rogatica. There were no professional soldiers or professional officers present. The unit was armed only with weapons that the Territorial Defence had held previously. Milovan Lelek was aware of the military detention facility which he visited on a number of occasions. He had no information that any of the detainees were subject to physical torture. Both military and civilian authorities took measures to enable Muslim civilians to charge -- to change their own place of residence temporarily if they wished. Milovan Lelek saw humanitarian aid convoys passing in the direction of Zepa and Gorazde. These convoys were escorted by UNPROFOR and were inspected at check-points. There were a number of incidents at check-points as the convoys carried assets that were not on the cargo manifest, including ammunition, radio devices, satellite navigation systems, rifles, sniper rifles, and so on. Helicopters would often pass over Borike who, it was later established, brought humanitarian aid into individual regions; however, the contents of the cargo could not be monitored and Muslim forces used this system to arm the villages. Milovan Lelek also discovered that members of the convoys found a better situation on the ground than described by the Muslim media and foreign reporters. In particular, there was a discrepancy in the reported size of the population. He considers that this was done to allow the inhabitants of Zepa to receive more humanitarian aid. The brigade command in Rogatica frequently issued authorisations for the seriously ill or wounded, especially children to be evacuated through Rogatica and some received medical care in the Rogatica health centre. And now I would ask the witness few questions in accordance with the decision of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, in keeping with the decision of the Chamber, I have to put a few questions to you relating to adjudicated facts, the adjudicated facts that you commented on in your statements, but we have to lead this live. I will ask my advisor to read them and then I will put my questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, with -- either --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, shall I hear from you first or -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Maybe you could hear from me first and that would make it easier. We could either maybe take about a five-minute break in which we could print out for Dr. Karadzic the text of the adjudicated facts so he could put them to the witness, or I could from my computer put those texts to the witness. So whichever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: As I alluded to before, I just don't think this is an appropriate way to elicit the evidence. The witness was in the municipality at the time, had a position in the army, should simply be asked what he knows about certain events. He should not be presented with evidence for his comment. It's just a leading and suggestive way of eliciting the evidence, and there's just no need to do it this way. He should just simply be asked what he knows and how.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After eliciting the evidence from the witness, do you oppose to putting the adjudicated fact to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, depending on the answer of the witness there may be something that arises that would require some specific piece of evidence to be put to him for clarification, but in general I just don't -- I mean, it's really a matter of ultimately argument for the accused at the end of the -- at the end of the case to argue that the adjudicated facts should be rejected. This seems to be a -- sort of an argumentative way of eliciting the evidence and I just don't see any need for it to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There's nothing leading or suggestive about asking a witness, for example: By the beginning of 1992 Rajko Kusic, a prominent SDS leader in Rogatica and a member of the SDS Main Board, had formed a paramilitary unit composed of 45 to 50 Serbs, among them SDS supporters from Rogatica municipality; is that true? I don't see anything wrong with doing it that way and that will be the most efficient and clear way. And if the witness wants to elaborate on -- if we want to ask him further questions as to how he knows or what he says when he gives an answer, we can do that; and if the Prosecutor wants to pursue that, they can do that. But there's simply nothing wrong with putting questions like that to the witness and that's the most efficient way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you wish to add anything, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber sees no difficulty with the way Mr. Robinson suggests. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, in a different trial it was established that in the beginning of 1992 Rajko Kusic, as a prominent SDS leader, along with being a member of the SDS Main Board, formed a paramilitary unit made up of 45 to 50 Serbs, including SDS followers from Rogatica. Can you tell us which part, if any, of this is true and what exactly Rajko Kusic formed?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I worked in the Territorial Defence staff until 1992, and I know well that the TO staff at the time had eight employees. Out of the eight, six were Muslim and two were Serb. In March 1992, the decision was made for the staff to be divided into the Serb and Muslim parts. The Muslim part remained in the hitherto premises of the TO staff, whereas the Serbian staff, including Rajko Kusic and the two Serb members, went to Borike village and set up the Serbian TO staff there. There were around 20 members of that staff but also some volunteers arrived from Serbia, people whose parents lived in the area of Borike, and they came deciding to join the Territorial Defence. I maintain it was not a paramilitary unit. It was a legally established Territorial Defence unit. That's all I have, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did this division of the TO staff occur? Was it a unilateral decision or by agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: By agreement. The TO staff as it existed then decided to divide into the Serbian and the Muslim parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was the task, the purpose of the Serbian part?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: The task of the Serbian part was to protect the civilian population in the villages populated by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was the task of the Muslim part?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Muslims immediately began setting up their own Territorial Defence because earlier, as I said in my statement, they had already set up the Green Berets; and later Mehmed Agic formed a TO staff for the Muslim part and they also rallied a certain number of Muslims, armed them, and protected their villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it is of assistance to the parties, it was adjudicated fact 2994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you this --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is also held to be established in a different case that Rajko Kusic and Svetozar Selinovic, president of the municipal SDS, wanted a division of the municipality as well as a division of the police force in the Territorial Defence in Rogatica and that in March 1992 Muslim negotiators agreed to that, intending to prevent a war. What would you have to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I was not in Rogatica then, but I know that in Srevgrad [phoen] in February the police station was divided into Muslim and Serbs -- Serb parts and the TO staff was divided in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it consensual or did the Serb side force the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: No, it was done by agreement. Both sides agreed of their own free will to divide both the police station and the TO staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is the next adjudicated fact, 2495.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: While the Defence is conferring I'd just like to point out that adjudicated facts 2495 does not appear to be among the facts that was covered in the statement. I think this exercise should be limited to only what facts we have notice of in the statement, so only those facts should count.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was just telling Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm sorry, I thought it was between 94, or rather, 494 and 500. I will stick to those that have been mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Also another adjudicated fact reads that sometime on the 4th or 5th March around 50 men in camouflage uniforms armed with automatic rifles including six members of the reserve police gathered in the Serbian village of Borike, proclaimed themselves to be the Serbian police, and continued to tour majority Serb villages in the municipality, shoot in the air, and intimidate the Muslim population. What can you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: No police was formed. Those were just members of the Territorial Defence formed by the Serbian municipality of Rogatica. As I said, those 20 men from Rogatica and those who came from Serbia, and there was no intimidation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say there was no intimidation, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I mean there was no intimidation of the Muslim population, that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In a different trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you also may ask the witness how he knew.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How come you know that there was no intimidation of Muslims and can you say where it was that they were and how they could intimidate Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
