utterances.text: At that time they were only in Borike. Borike is predominantly Serb populated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How could you know where they were? What was your position then? Were you in the municipal structures?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: No. I've already said while I was staying with my parents in the village, from Borike couriers often came to tell us what the situation was, whether we needed any help, because my village was also surrounded by Muslims. And I was in the village together with my parents and I stood guard together with the locals from that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In some other trial there was this adjudicated fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably for record you -- maybe I thought mention the number of the adjudicated fact, for future reference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The previous one was 2500, the one about intimidation and weapons. And now we are talking about adjudicated fact 2499, where it says that it was established that Kusic and the SDS ordered all Muslims in the municipality of Rogatica to hand over their weapons as they were threatened with arrest and expulsion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you know about this and what the situation was and who was where and who could disarm who?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Rajko Kusic didn't threaten anyone then. There were villages, Muslim villages, that had declared their loyalty to the Serb side, like, for example, Berkovici, Gucevo, Satorovici, Okruglo, Strmac, Burati. They were not carrying out any hostile activities against the Serb side. They were not firing at the Serb side. There was no problem coming from them. They remained loyal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was your attitude, the attitude of the Serbs and the Serb authorities towards them?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: For as long as these villages were loyal, for as long as there weren't any problems regarding these villages, our attitude was good. Our authorities regularly brought supplies to these villages, food supplies. I'll just give you one example, some of these villages that I mentioned here, that I see have been mentioned here, for example, Gucevo, the village and local commune of Gucevo. It's a village nearby Zakomo and Berkovici. These are two neighbouring villages. Between these two neighbouring villages there was a Muslim village, Oskoplje. The residents of Oskoplje often threatened Zakomo and Berkovici, and they attacked them by saying that they co-operated with the Serbs. On one occasion a resident of Zakomo came to the house of Luko Planojevic and asked him to try to provide transportation from there with the -- from the civilian authorities because they didn't dare live there any longer. They worried about their safety because of the Muslim threats. Then Radoje Planojevic, Luka's son, called the then-president of the Serb municipality and asked him to send a bus to that village so that the population of the village could leave. Even before the bus arrived, Muslims had gathered around Luka's house and then they disappeared together with the Serbs. They thanked them for their support, and they asked them to take care of their property, their houses and everything else, and they thanked them. From there they were moved to the collection centre, and after that at their own wish they changed the place where they were staying. After the war they started returning to the village of Zakomo because their houses hadn't been looted or anything. May I just say something else? Maybe this will take a bit longer. I would like to respond in terms of all the villages that are mentioned here. For example, we had the village of Strmac. It was loyal up until on one occasion near their village Rajak Ljubinac was killed from an ambush. One day before that they brought food supplies to that village, and the next day near that village on the road between Strmac and Rogatica they were killed from an ambush, then the villagers themselves asked to leave that village. That's what they asked the village guards and the Serb authorities to do. They didn't want to go to other villages, Kopljevici, Pokrivenik, and further on towards Gorazde. We also have the villages --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sorry, was this a Serb or a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Strmac was a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps we'll go back to that but let's finish with this. In line 22 the witness said they embraced with the Serbs not disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: They embraced the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Maybe we'll get to that question in some other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd just like to ask you this, these villages that remained loyal and handed over their weapons were in which territory, Serb or Muslim, in terms of the municipality of Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, Mr. President. I don't know how this territory was divided, where it was the Muslim municipality and where it was the Serb municipality --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the end of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Pause, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any villages that were Muslim villages which were not asked to hand over weapons and which did not give any weapons? What happened there? Which villages are these? And what was their situation?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: There's the village of Madjer. They were never asked to hand over their weapons and they did not. They lived next door to a Serb village. They lived there all the time and they received regular food supplies and they even got more food supplies than the Serb population. They stayed there all the way up until -- well, I can't remember exactly the month, but until the conflict broke out in the area of Dobromirovici when Ristic, Vojin and Ristic, Dusan were slaughtered by Muslims. These were two old men who were 80 then. And Radenko was killed at his door-step.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: This is too fast for interpretation of each and every word. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, can I advise you to put a pause between the question and the answer and speak slow for the benefit of the interprets. They are saying you are speaking a bit too fast. Can you repeat from where you mentioned door-step, Radenko.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that this Muslim population lived there safely up until the Muslim extremists slaughtered Ristic, Vojin and Ristic, Dusanka. They were 80 years old. Ristic, Radenko was killed on his door-step. Soon after that in the village of Pesurici, that is about 6 or 7 kilometres away from there, they killed 12 civilians. At the time they were involved in agricultural work. Two elderly women were locked up in their houses and they torched these houses and these women burned together with their houses. After that, the Muslim population of the village of Madjer did not feel safe there any longer and they told our village guards who were there and who saw them every day, right, they said that they wanted to leave Madjer. However, since Madjer is only, say, 3 or 4 kilometres away from Kopljevici and Pokrivenik, I don't know exactly how many kilometres, they also asked that they move further on towards Kopljevici and Pokrivenik and further on towards Gorazde. And their wish was granted all the time their houses remained intact. They were not torched. I heard the testimony of a witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters did not hear the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- who testified here, and he said afterwards they went to their village to bring food because the Muslims in Pokrivenik and further on in Ustipraca did not give him any food because they were accused of co-operating with the Serb side. The village was torched later when a Serb village was torched too, a Serb village that was in the neighbourhood, and I've already said they took care of each other. But when this Serb village was torched, later on the Muslim village of Madjer was torched as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, could you repeat the name of the witness you referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hurko Sefik. I read his father's statement. I don't know whether he testified here, but he did best. He explained how they took care of each other, the Muslims and the Serbs there in these neighbouring villages Leleci and Madjer, that they took care of the locals in the other village. And when the municipality gave food they gave more food; the Serb municipality gave more food to the Muslims than to the Serbs there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In relation to Vragolovi and Muslim concentrations, was anybody issuing any threats there? Was anybody trying to disarm them?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: No one threatened them there in Madjer. They lived there normally until these two incidents happened, the ones that I already mentioned, Ristic and Pesurici, those two incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to draw your attention to 1971. That's the number of the adjudicated fact. It says here that it was established that with the intention of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, what's the number of the adjudicated fact?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1971 [In English] 1971.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This should be -- this seems to be some mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, my mistake. I do apologise. I'd like to draw your attention to 2503, adjudicated fact 2503, and now I'd like to put that to you. I'd like to tell you what is considered adjudicated there. In the night between the 12th and 13th of May, 1992, in the area of Zivaljevina, in the municipality of Rogatica, the zone of Zivaljevina was shelled by mortar fire and anti-aircraft weapons. Artillery shells from Pljesivica and Seljani --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the adjudicated facts, the original text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What can you tell us, when did the fighting start in the municipality of Rogatica --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: The fighting in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue. Yes. Yes, please continue, Mr. Lelek.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fighting in the municipality of Rogatica started on the 22nd of May. That is to say that was two or three days -- two days after the killing of our first soldier, Mihajlovic Drazenko. Before the fighting there was none of that, but the date mentioned by the President now is the date that was taken from Mehmet Agic's statement that you have here in this court. Mehmet Agic says that the first clashes in Rogatica broke out on the 9th of May. And he says exactly when an aggressor soldier was killed in the area of Laza, he says on the 9th of May. Now, was this a typo or it was a mistake anyway. And now these ten days. So the date, the 12th and 13th, that is not right. There couldn't have been any armed conflict before the 22nd -- actually, this is what Mehmet Agic also confirmed on the 9th of May when the first enemy soldier was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the practice there? Did it ever happen that the Serb side would shell a village, a Muslim village, from which fire should not be opened or was not opened?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Mehmet Agic said in his statement the 12th or 13th, but I am saying for sure that it is the 22nd of May when we tried to get our dead soldier's body out and the only road through which we could get there to get the soldier's body out was from Rudo towards Zlatni Do and further to Laze. From Rudo to Laze it's about 2 or 3 kilometres, and the area of Zlatni Do there was a large concentration of Muslim forces. When they were leaving Zlatni Do we found fuel, water tanks, and some vehicles and they went further on from there, and of course we did not fire at a populated area. We had to liberate the road in order to get Drazenko Mihajlovic's body out. When we tried to get the body out, there was fighting on both sides, and it's just if they consider that to be shelling. But as for anything else I really have nothing more to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like us to see what is adjudicated fact 2505 and it says there that the Serb police and others in olive-green-grey camouflage uniforms moved from their houses, those who did not obey the orders to leave and go to the high school centre, and they separated men from women and they beat the men. What can you say about the high school centre and about this allegation and the way in which people got to the high school centre and how they were treated?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: People came to the high school centre of their own free will from the town when the town was -- after the events with Mihajlovic happened. When there was fighting in the town, later those who did not want any fighting would voluntarily surrender to the building. From the villages which were loyal, the citizens also expressed their desire to come to the collection centre because they were afraid of the revenge by Muslim extremists because they kept threatening them that they were providing data to the Serbian army, that they were collaborating with them and of their own free will they expressed the desire to come to the collection centre, to the high school centre, because they were able to then select their place of residence of their own free will. They were not forced there by anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who controlled that part of town from which people transferred to the high school centre and under whose control was the rest of Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: The centre of the town throughout the whole time belonged to --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I just ask for a time-frame for this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us when the high school centre was formed -- I mean, when did it start receiving these people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, I'm not sure if the entire answer of the witness to the previous question was fully reflected. The centre of the town throughout the whole time belonged to who, Mr. Lelek?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole time the centre of town up until the 23rd of July, 1992, when Rogatica was liberated was under the control of the Muslims. The northern and the southern parts belonged to the Serbs, that is, the Donje Polje and the Karanfil neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us when was the high school centre set up? When was it turned into this collection centre and how long did this go on for?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I cannot know the exact date because I wasn't in Rogatica then. I cannot really know the exact date when the centre was opened, this collection centre in the high school, but I know that it was operating until August 1992, end of August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you able to tell the Trial Chamber what happened with the civilians who had been in the high school centre up until that time? What happened after the liberation of Rogatica? Where did they go?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: They expressed their wish where they wanted to go, in which direction they wanted to go. Up until that time, they were treated there. They had the same three meals that our troops had on the lines, it was the same food. There was civilian police standing in front of the high school centre, in front of the collection centre. The centre was secured or guarded by the civilian police. Afterwards, when a sufficient number of civilians had gathered there, when they said where they wanted to go, transport would be organised for them and then they would leave the high school centre in -- under escort by the civilian police and they would go in the direction where they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did anybody else return to these villages where there was no fighting which were loyal?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: There was no return to those villages. At the time they did not wish to return to villages because they were afraid of revenge from Muslims because they had allegedly co-operated with the Turks -- no, with the Serbs, I apologise, and while they were staying in the high school centre when the town was liberated they were able to go to their houses freely, take something that was left in their apartments, food and things like that. But before Rogatica was liberated, they did not dare to do that because of the Muslim forces. Other than Muslim families, there was the Neskovic family, the Gavric family, and there were three or four Serb families there also at this collection centre --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, the other participants cannot tell by the surnames which ethnic group a family belongs to.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: There were the Gavric, Neskovic and Brusin families of Serb ethnicity. These were families who were Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And so what would have happened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Witness -- I'm sorry, interpreters noted that they did not understand the last sentence of the witness's previous answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that refer to the families that I mentioned? Is that the last sentence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Other than the Muslim inhabitants which responded to the summons to report to the collection centre because they would be provided with all safety there, that nobody would be abused there, there were also three Serbian families that reported in: The Neskovic family, the Gavric family and the Brusin family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask you now to look at adjudicated fact 2506 which states that later local Serbs under the leadership of Rajko Kusic captured up to 1100 Muslims from Rogatica and held them at the high school centre in that same centre thus. Are you able to tell us what was the nature and status of the people who were in the centre?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: After the conflict broke out, after the first armed conflicts broke out, a few days after that most of the population, Serb and Muslim, left Rogatica. A part of the Muslim population went in the direction of Madjer, Kopljevici, Pokrivenik and on towards Gorazde, and one column of Muslims then went towards the village or Vragolovi. The Serb population left the town at the time. They went to their families and nearby villages which were under Serb control and which were close by and they were safer. Women and children also went to relatives in Serbia if they had any there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And these people who came to the high school centre, were they detainees or prisoners in any sense of the word?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: They were not prisoners or detainees. One knows how you treat prisoners and how you treat the civilian population. They received food three times a day, the same food that our troops on the line received. It means that they were treated as civilians and not as prisoners. We know what a prisoner looks like when he's released and we know what civilians look like when they come out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you able to tell us if there were 1100 of them there as it is stated in the adjudicated fact?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact number, but I state with full responsibility that there were no more than 200 to 250, that is the number of them that passed through the centre up to the period in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And adjudicated fact 2510 says that the Serbian forces detained up to 1100 Muslim civilians in the Rogatica secondary school where they mistreated them, beat them, raped them in the period from June to August 1992. What are you able to say about this assertion?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I did not come. I never entered to the collection centre -- I never entered the collection centre throughout that period. I know there was the civilian police there so that they would prevent anyone from entering the compound and mistreating the civilian population because frequently Serbs, Arkan, Seselj's men would come to Rogatica. We were afraid that they would go in. But whenever we found out that these men came to Rogatica, we would arrest them and expel them from Rogatica. So the police was there to guard the civilians so that nobody from outside would enter and mistreat them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was it established or talked about any beatings and rapes in the high school centre and could the Muslims who were walking around the town bring this information?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: There were no rapes. I couldn't go in to see if there were any or not, but the Muslims who would come out to walk around the town could not disseminate such information because they couldn't walk around until the town was liberated. They didn't dare come out because of the Muslims, the local Muslims. They could not, those who surrendered, go out and walk around Rogatica until it was liberated in 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the whole date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Earlier you mentioned security --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Still both of you are talking a bit too fast without giving a pause. The interpreters couldn't hear the last part of the answer, in particular the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The date when it was liberated.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes, I will repeat. The civilian population, both Serbs and Muslims, who were in the collection centre in the high school were able to go out freely to walk around the town only after the 27th of July when Rogatica was liberated. Before that date, they did not dare come out, neither of them, because they were afraid of Muslim extremists who could have attacked them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Earlier you mentioned the police who were providing security. So I would like to ask you about what you know regarding adjudicated fact 2507 which states that it was established that guards with machine-guns, with machine-gun nests -- and machine-gun nests were placed around the school and that the detainees were informed that the surrounding area was mined. Are you able to tell us who and in which way guarded the centre and from whom? Was it to prevent people from going in and out or from people coming in?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: The civilian police was there posted. There were no machine-gun nests there or anything like that and there were no mines that were laid around the school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How do you know that? You told us you didn't enter there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I didn't enter the premises of the high school. They couldn't have placed the mines inside the school, but around the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you walk around town and close to the high school centre at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I passed perhaps once or twice around the -- or by the high school centre and then I couldn't go any further, I didn't dare, because there were Muslim forces there. I didn't notice any machine-gun nests. I would have noticed them if there were any. I would have also noticed the minefield if there was one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned the village of Vragolovi. And adjudicated fact 2513 states that by the end of 1992 more than ten mosques in the Rogatica municipality were destroyed by mines. That includes the Rogatica mosque, Arnaudija mosque, three mosques in Vragolovi in that area west of Rogatica, including the mosque in Vragolovi itself. Are you able to tell us who controlled those sectors where allegedly Serbs blew up these mosques?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I know about two mosques that were in Rogatica, both of them were in the centre of town and both of them were under the control of the Muslim forces. I don't know which mosque it was, Muhadija [phoen], I know one mosque was hit by a tank shell because it was hit by a tank shell. There was a -- somebody going behind Karanfil in Donje Polje to pull out a wounded fighter and then right next to the mosque, some 5, 6, or 10 metres at the most a tank went over an anti-personnel mine and a person was killed, Radisa something, and then we found out that there was a sniper nest on the minaret of the mosque. The Green Berets in Rogatica would assemble around the mosque and then what was noticed was that they were bringing out anti-tank mines from the mosque. And when our driver was killed we eliminated the mosque in order to get rid of the anti-tank artillery or ordnance. Then 10 to 15 metres away from a machine-gun nest in the course of the fighting we saw that there was one there, and it's possible that when we were hitting it we also struck the mosque.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Vragolovi there was a greater concentration of Muslim forces. I don't know what happened in the village itself, but I know that throughout the whole time we did draw the attention of our fighters to the fact that they should not destroy any religious facilities. As for the places that were under the control of the Serbian forces in Rogatica there was the Catholic church which remained intact throughout the fighting and it's still standing there. In the parts of town controlled by the Muslim forces, there was a synagogue and that was knocked down by the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And these two mosques that were hit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I will leave it to you as to the intervention from the interpreter, saying that they didn't hear the last sentence before their intervention.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that everything was recorded in the transcript. The witness said that the synagogue which was under the control of the Muslims was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then let's continue, but please speak slowly, Mr. Lelek. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the second mosque that you mentioned that you said that it was hit by a shell that fell short, was this in Rogatica? Which mosque were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I'm talking about both of the mosques. This one, I don't know how you named it, Muhadija or something, one of them was hit by a tank and this other one was hit by a mortar shell because some 10 metres away from it there was the machine-gun nests of theirs. Both of them were in the centre of town, in that sector of town, which was under the control of the Muslim forces and that was an area where combat was going on. There was combat in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Serbian forces, did they control Vragolovi and these villages around Vragolovi where allegedly these mosques were destroyed; and if they did, in which period was that that they were controlling those sectors?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I don't know when they were knocked down. I said that one-third of the population, soldiers and regular people, went to the village of Vragolovi. I had the opportunity to read the statement of Meho Mehargic [phoen]. I mentioned that a number of times. And there he says that from the village of Vragolovi where there were a large concentration of Muslim forces he brought about 80 people from there to the centre of town and he joined them to the forces that were defending town, some 120 men, that he brought them to town, that he deployed them to the Ljun [phoen] hill which is a hill right in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say there were quite a few people, regular people and soldiers, what kind of population are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Vragolovi village was a Muslim village and all the population from Rogatica villages went in the direction of Kopljevici, some went to Vragolovi, others continued towards Gorazde. And over there, there were armed Muslim units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was adjudicated fact 2513. Just one more last question: Which places of worship or cultural buildings were destroyed in that area?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I've already told you about the two mosques destroyed in Rogatica. I know that the Catholic church which was in the area of responsibility of our forces remained intact, and I don't know about the other mosques really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure the question was interpreted correctly. I'm interested, what, if anything, was destroyed in the Serb-controlled zone? Did Serbs destroy any places of worship or cultural buildings?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: No. There were only two mosques in town but that area was controlled by the Muslim forces. There were two mosques in town, in the centre of town, and they were destroyed while the Muslim forces were there and they were probably destroyed in the exchange of fire in combat. For the rest, all I know that our troops were regularly warned that they must not destroy it -- destroy places of worship and they obeyed and we know that from the fact that the Catholic church remained standing and intact in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Excellencies, regarding adjudicated facts. I have no questions until re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it the Defence is not tendering 1D6833 referred to in para 12?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I would like you to redact that part, the last part of para 12 starting from the part "that these were lies and fabrications" as well as paras 27 to 32 be redacted. Yes, Mr. Lelek --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we'll do that and before we start the cross-examination if I could just make one statement just so it's clear to everyone as an issue of notice, since this is the first time we've dealt exclusively with adjudicated facts and that is that as the Chamber in the Mladic case held: Once evidence is introduced to rebut an adjudicated fact, the Prosecution can no longer rely on the presumption and must introduce evidence in support of that fact either in its case in chief or in its rebuttal case. So it's our position with respect to these adjudicated facts that once evidence has been offered, such as has been done today, that the presumption no longer applies. And I just wanted to alert the Prosecution and the Chamber of that so that it doesn't hear that for the first time in our closing submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's your submission. Yes, Mr. Robinson. Yes, as you have noted, Mr. Lelek, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in most part in the form of writing, i.e., your written statement in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And just one minor note before I commence if I could ask the Defence to provide us - it doesn't have to be at this moment - with a citation to the Mladic reference because obviously that submission is something we will have to take into consideration. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Lelek.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now just as a preliminary matter in the course of your evidence today I noticed you referred to quite a number of witness statements that people have given about these events, and I take it from that that you have followed legal proceedings here and in Bosnia in relation to events in Rogatica during the war. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I just? I would appreciate if we would be notified or given the documents that are going to be used during the cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: We're having some technical problems here. We'll get them out as soon as we possibly can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's proceed. Or if it is convenient we can take an early break.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, it will take us a few moments to get the cross-examination documents out, so it's up to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, as long as they don't use any of the documents we can continue up until that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I can say in the next few minutes I may use P3265, but that's an associated exhibit so it shouldn't cause any problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, would you like me to repeat my question or can you answer it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: My question was whether you've been following legal proceedings here and/or in Bosnia in relation to events in Rogatica during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I followed while in Rogatica the trials taking place here at this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it's clear from your statement that you were the assistant commander for operations and training in the Rogatica Brigade from late May 1992 until early 1994 and then you became Chief of Staff, a position you held until the Dayton Accords. Now, as far -- to the best of your knowledge, during the war were any members of the Rogatica Brigade punished for any crimes committed against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I know two were convicted, Spiro, I can't remember his first name, Spiro is his nickname, and I know that --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, I think you're referring to a case in Bosnia that was some years after the war. I'm talking about during the war. Between 1992 and 1995 were any members of the Rogatica Brigade punished for any crimes against non-Serbs during that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember that. At the beginning you said yourself I was assistant commander for operations and training, and there was an investigating judge who questioned suspects. So I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And in your statement you explained that around the end of May you left your village of Dobromirovici and at that point you joined the Serb TO in Borike, and that's at paragraphs 8 and 9. And then you talked in your statement and today about the attack carried out by Serb forces on the 22nd of May. On the 22nd of May, were you still in your village in Dobromirovici or had you gone to Borike to join the TO by that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I went to Borike and joined the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So on the 22nd of May were you physically in Borike?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And at paragraph 10 of your statement you said that when you arrived in Borike part of the command moved to the Sladara building in Rogatica, but that you stayed in Borike and you were tasked with organising the defence towards Zepa. So I take it from that that you were not involved in operations in Rogatica town and the surrounding villages because you were involved in defensive activities towards Zepa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Well, I, as a member of the brigade command, naturally had to attend meetings of the brigade that were held sometimes in Rogatica, sometimes in Borike, because I had to take part in preparing the combat documentation and all the activities of the brigade. So if I was in Borike that doesn't mean I couldn't participate in the work of the brigade command because there was the assistant commander for operations and training, assistant commanders for other affairs, and it was desirable for all members of the command to be present at the meetings unless somebody was absolutely unable to due to other commitments.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we kindly ask the witness to speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lelek, you've been asked to speak a little -- move a little more closely towards the microphone. Thank you. So -- but in terms of your practical involvement in operations, did you have any hands-on practical involvement in operations in Rogatica town and the surrounding villages during the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: No, I did not take part in operations. As I said, I took part in the evening meetings and I would take part in debates at these meetings, but I did not take part in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I think in your evidence today you made clear that there was no shelling of populated areas and you made clear that this -- any shelling that took place occurred during exchanges of fire and ongoing fighting. Is that a correct understanding of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I've said that we, when we had to pull out the body of the late Mihajlovic, there occurred an exchange of fire. There was no shelling. And since you're asking, when we were pulling out the body of the late Mihajlovic we opened fire in the direction of Kopljevici and Trnovo because we had received intelligence that one Serbian family had been left behind alone encircled by the Muslims. And unfortunately, since we were short of personnel, a lot of men were engaged as village guards, we were unable to reach that family. And after a while that family was practically butchered. It's the family of Mico Obradovic. He was killed, his wife was killed, his son, his brother-in-law, and late Danijela, 17 year old, she was raped before she was murdered. We tried to move towards that village but we did not have enough forces and we just failed in saving that family.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The details of the woman being disembowelled did not find their way into the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I repeat, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You just confirm, it said here in the record that the 17-year-old girl was raped and then killed, but you said more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it was a real massacre over that family. The father, the mother, son, brother-in-law, and daughter were killed, daughter Danijela, 17 year old, she was first raped and then she was eviscerated. The others were massacred. So if your record says they were murdered, it's not murdered because that would be killed from a fire-arm. They were massacred.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, if you could concentrate on questions. The question was whether the shelling took place during the exchange of fire. Do you understand that, sir? Please continue, Ms. Gustafson. Just one more question and then we'll have a lunch break.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, just so I'm clear, you said in the operation to pull out Mihajlovic's body that there was no shelling. Is it your evidence that there was no shelling by Serb forces on the 22nd of May?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: At that time we had one anti-aircraft gun and, of course, when we set out to pull out the body of the late Mihajlovic and met with resistance we opened fire but not in the populated area, only in that segment of the road. We targeted not the populated area. We fired in order to open the way to the infantry. The infantry couldn't pass because it was met with fire and you know that every infantry attack is preceded by the artillery preparation of the terrain but not against populated areas. There was no shelling that means. We just had one anti-aircraft gun that we fired in order to get out the body of the late Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could just follow-up, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, witness after witness in this case, including Defence witness Mile Ujic, who was the Chief of Staff of the brigade at the time, testified to a major shelling attack on the 22nd of May; Sefik Hurko testified that on the 22nd of May fire was opened on all the Muslim villages in Rogatica municipality, that's at T 18223; Elvir Pasic gave evidence that on the 22nd of May Rogatica was attacked with artillery, anti [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we get a reference, please --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm giving the reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. She is giving references. But could you speak slow.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Elvir Pasic gave evidence that beginning on the 22nd of May Rogatica was attacked with artillery, anti-aircraft weaponry and infantry weapons; that's P59 at T 857 to 860. KDZ051 testified that the shelling of Rogatica town began at noon on the 21st or 22nd of May; P3405 paragraph 30. KDZ607 described the shelling of Zlatni Do, an exclusively Muslim settlement of a hundred houses on the 22nd of May; P3289, paragraph 11. Alija Isakovic gave evidence that Rogatica town was first shelled on the 22nd of May with mortars anti-aircraft guns, tanks, artillery, and heavy machine-guns; P127 and P128. KDZ606 described an all-out shelling attack on Rogatica town and villages that were populated mainly by Muslims on the 22nd of May, 1992; P3279, paragraph 90. And as I mentioned, when Mile Ujic was shown the document P3265, which is a combat report for the 22nd of May, he described this as a shelling as well as an infantry attack. It was a combined operation. That's at transcript page 33460.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lelek, your evidence that you had one anti-aircraft gun that you used on one occasion on one part of the road just doesn't stand up next to the weight of all of this contrary evidence, does it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: There's no way we could have opened artillery fire on the town on the 22nd because at that time there was still Serb population in the centre of the town. Only a day or two after that event both the Serb and Muslim population was seized with fear and then they started to pull out. I told you that in response to the previous question. So we couldn't have shelled the town on the 22nd because in the centre of the town there was still Serb civilians. Only a day or two after the 22nd did the civilian population pull out. There was no shelling then. At that time we had that anti-aircraft gun and perhaps some mortars, but we did not shell the centre of the town because there was Serb population there still. We did open fire from the anti-aircraft gun but not on the populated area. That was an area with a great concentration of Muslim forces and that was the axis of Rudo-Zlatni Do where the body of late Mihajlovic was. And of course if we wanted to pull it out of course we had to open up that road using infantry, and in order to use infantry we had to first open fire from the anti-aircraft gun and perhaps 60-millimetre mortars because every infantry attack has to be prepared before that by artillery. But there was certainly no shelling of the town then.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I assume Your Honours would like to take the lunch break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break for 45 minutes and resume at 20 past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.32 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And just before I start I should have mentioned this at the outset, the 45 minutes that I was granted was given to me before the additional information was provided in the statement that we've now heard live, and before that information was included in the witness's evidence I was confident I could complete in 45 minutes. Now I'm quite confident that I can't and I hope the Chamber will grant me more than the normal level --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you're confident you could conclude in an hour?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's my aim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, just before we broke for lunch you said that on the 22nd of May the brigade had only one anti-aircraft gun. A few moments later you clarified that slightly then; you said you may have had one or two 60-millimetre mortars. My question for you is: When, if ever, did the brigade obtain larger-calibre mortars, 82-millimetres or 120-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: In the Territorial Defence before the war we had infantry weapons. We had these anti-aircraft guns. We had 82-millimetre mortars and 60-millimetre mortars. When the Army of Republika Srpska was founded on the 19th of May, 1992, then from Uzamnica near Visegrad we brought some infantry weapons, some 82-millimetre and 60-millimetre mortars and an anti-aircraft gun because the commander of the republican territorial defence staff before the war issued an order to the effect that for safety reasons all the weapons of the Territorial Defence be relocated to storage facilities. We moved ours to Uzamnica near Visegrad, and it was only --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. My time is very limited. I asked you a very precise question which was: When did the Rogatica Brigade obtain larger-calibre mortars, 82-millimetre or 120-millimetres. I'm not interested in all the background and all the reasons. I just want to know the date, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: End of April, 82-millimetre and 60-millimetre, end of April when Visegrad was liberated. As for 120-millimetres, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's fine. That's very clear. Thank you. I'd like to now ask you about -- some questions about the secondary school. Now, you made clear that you didn't actually enter the secondary school. You said that you passed by it a few times when the Muslims were located there. Did you ever speak to any of the Muslims who were held at the secondary school centre?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I never saw anyone and never talked to anyone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone and speak slower.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 11 the witness side: I'm not sure when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you didn't hear, Mr. Lelek, you are requested again by the interpreters to speak much slower and come to the microphone a little bit closer.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Your answer is clear that you never spoke to any of the Muslims held there. Now, you gave substantial amount of evidence about what happened there. You said the Muslims came of their own free will, they came from loyal villages because they were afraid of revenge by Muslims. You said from the school they expressed their wish of where they wanted to go and transport was arranged for them under escort by civilian police. You said there were no more than 250 people there. There was a fear that Arkan or Seselj's men would mistreat people there, but they were arrested and expelled. Nobody was raped. And when you went by the high school once or twice you saw that there were no machine-gun nests there. Now, in 2004 you were asked about the secondary school by the Rogatica police and you gave them a very different version of events than you gave the Court today. You told them you'd never been to the school when the Muslims were kept there, as you did today, but you said you'd also never been to that area. And you said that all you knew about what happened at the school was what you heard from some people you didn't know, and that was that it was used as a collection centre for Bosniaks where Bosniaks were kept and from where they were transported to territory under ABiH control. Now, that's what you told the Rogatica police in 2004 was all you knew -- that was all you knew about the secondary school; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Well, I say to this day that I never entered the secondary school. I came to the forestry buildings, that is opposite the secondary school. As for the area where the school is, I never entered the compound. I never entered the school building.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay if we could have 65 ter 24652, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, while that's being called up, this is a document that was not disclosed to us previously and we have had an order from the Chamber with respect to prior statements from witnesses from the municipalities that have been ordered to redisclose to us. But that order applied to a certain number of witnesses that were associated with Crisis Staffs and this witness is not one of them, so there's no violation of that order. But the Prosecution has been endeavouring to provide us with the statements and documents authored by our other witnesses from the municipalities who were not subject to that order, and we refrained from asking for any supplemental order covering those people based on the Prosecution's practice and undertaking to disclose those statements to us. And Mr. Tieger has advised me that this was not disclosed to us by oversight and not by any design or any change in that policy. So we're not asking for any remedy at this point, but we just wanted to make a record of the fact that this document had not previously been disclosed to us and we wouldn't expect that this would recur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue. Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to the second page in the B/C/S -- sorry, the second page in the English, first page in the B/C/S and about halfway down the large paragraph in the middle of the B/C/S and at the top of the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is the note of your interview with the police in 2004. It says: "He also did not know anything about the activities of establishing collection centres in the territory of the municipality referring to Sladara, Rasadnik, Parohijski Dom elementary school and secondary school before he came to Borike ..." And then the next sentence it says: "He heard from some persons he did not know that there were collection centres in the town area in the above-mentioned facilities where citizens of Bosniak nationality were kept and from where they were later transported by buses to the territory under ABiH control. "He also said he did not know that the persons in the collection centres were mistreated or tortured in any way. During the time the above-mentioned centres existed, he did not come into the areas where they were located." So, basically, Mr. Lelek, although you've given very detailed evidence about what happened at the Rogatica secondary school today, in 2004 you said you didn't know anything about it except that it was where citizens of Bosniak nationality were kept and later transferred to ABiH-controlled territory and that you didn't even go into the area where the high school was located, contrary to what you've told the Chamber today. Now, this is what you told the police in 2004; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: When I say to this day I say now that I did not enter the premises of the sedentary school and I did not enter the area where that school is, I didn't enter the compound. I only came to the building opposite the school where the forestry organisation was.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you agree that all the information you provided to the police in 2004 about the secondary school centre is reflected in the passage I just read to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I didn't understand what you were saying. Which paragraph is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I just read out to you what you told the police in 2004 - if we could go to the previous page in the B/C/S - that all you knew about the school was from people you didn't know and that was that citizens of Bosniak nationality were kept there and they were transported to ABiH-controlled territory from there. You didn't tell the police in 2004 anything else about the secondary school, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's correct, that this note reflects what you told the police?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I said to the police then that I did not come there, there where the school is located, that I never entered that school. And of course later, as I was preparing for this, I knew that I came opposite the school building. But when they asked whether I came exactly to where the school is I said I did not enter that area, the school area, and I did not enter the building or the compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6151, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lelek, you insisted today that the Muslims at the secondary school centre came there of their own free will. A unit commander in your brigade, Radosav Ljubinac, was convicted in 2007 for forcibly transferring Muslims from Seljani village to the secondary school and from there to Sarajevo, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I was not aware of that event. Later on I found out that he was tried and convicted, but then I did not know that he brought anyone from Seljani, although in my personal opinion -- maybe it's better if he brought them, unless it was forcibly, to the secondary school because the late Mihajlovic whom we've mentioned several times during this trial, he's from the village of Seljani. It's perhaps only a kilometre or two away from the Muslim part and perhaps there could have been revenge, perhaps there could have been revenge on the part of the father of the boy who was only 20 years old and who was killed. So then maybe that is the reason why they were brought to the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, in that -- in relation to your last comment let's go to P6106, page 26. This is the judgement that convicted Mr. Ljubinac and he was convicted for a number of different crimes. If we could go to page 26, one of them was the one I mentioned to you. This is where the discussion begins and if we could go to the next page. This is only in English so I will read the relevant passage to you, begins near the end of the first large paragraph. It says: "So on 3rd and 4th August ... they," and this refers to the Muslim residents of Seljani "were gathered ... when under the excuse that they should be transferred in order to be protected from shelling soon to come, they were addressed by the soldiers and ordered to get onto the bus which belonged to their neighbour Radosav Ljubinac, the accused. That bus took them to the secondary school centre in Rogatica." The next paragraph says that all the witnesses identified Ljubinac as the driver. And in the next paragraph it says: "All the above mentioned witnesses agree that their forcible transfer commenced with arrival of a group of soldiers, including also some soldiers familiar to them, who informed them that due to a great attack being prepared on Seljani they all had to be transferred to a safe place. That transfer took place in the manner that they were loaded on the bus driven by their neighbour, Radosav Ljubinac, who also took them to the secondary school centre, Veljko Vlahovic, in Rogatica. There they were informed that they should stay two days until the shelling was over. "The fact is that in the secondary school centre they stayed for one or two days, that is until 5 August 1992 when instead of being returned to their homes because the 'shelling' should have been over at the time, they were separated. A number of them were loaded on buses and trucks and transferred to Hresa locality in Sarajevo and others including men and not only adult men were kept in the secondary school centre." Now, that is what happened to the Muslim residents of Seljani: They were taken by force to the secondary school centre, lied to, told that they would be able to return to their village, and instead were expelled to Sarajevo, except the men who continued to be detained; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot comment upon that because I'm not aware of those facts and I would not be in a position to give any comments on this. I know that Ljubinac was convicted. I don't know why. This is the first time I see this judgement and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first two pages of this document have been admitted. I'd like to add pages 26 and 27 to Exhibit P6106.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lelek, at paragraph 19 of your statement you said there was a military detention facility in Rasadnik which you visited several times, and you said that you saw some Muslims who you knew from before who were detained there and that you know that investigations were being conducted against them on various grounds. This is paragraph 19 of your statement. Could you please name the Muslims you saw at Rasadnik who you knew from before.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I wanted -- Hurko Fejzo, Hurko Sefik, that's the witness who testified here. I saw Suceska Sajin from Berkovici. I also saw from Berkovici two or three Kustores [phoen] but I cannot remember the names.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you said that you know that investigations were being conducted against the Muslims held at Rasadnik. What were these investigations for? What were they being investigated for?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Because they were suspects. They had weapons when some of the Muslim villages were searched. They said that they did not have any weapons. However, then weapons were found during the search. So investigations were therefore carried out against them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you know any Muslim held at Rasadnik who was ever formally charged with crime?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Well, I don't. I know only the ones I mentioned and none of them were there. I mean, I gave the four or five names of the persons I saw up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Lelek, it's true, is it not, that ordinary Muslim civilians were being held at Rasadnik; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Only those who were suspects were detained in Rasadnik. After the secondary school was closed, then I think only people from Berkovici were brought to Rasadnik and also those from the local commune of Gucevo because the collection centre of the secondary school was closed and we had to put them next door to our military detention. It wasn't one and the same thing because there is this other building right next to our military detention facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. There were women among the detainees, right, Muslim women?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I didn't see any. I didn't enter the collection centre when it was in the school or in Rasadnik. I only went to speak with our fighters who were escaping from the line and I went to talk to them. I didn't talk to anyone from Berkovici who were brought to the reception centre or the collection centre in Rasadnik except for these four that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay if we could go to P4867, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the counsel to slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, this document is a report from October 1994 on a prisoner exchange that took place between the 5th and 10th of October, 1994. And if we could go to page 4 of the English and the B/C/S. This is a -- the report is from the Federation side. And at the top of this list, the list which is at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S, it says: "The other side did not free all the persons from the signed list, namely ..." And the last name on the list, number 11 is Hanka Kustura. According to the Serbian side she died at the age of 101 while in Rogatica-Rasadnik prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to 65 ter 24647.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please be informed as to who signed this?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This report was admitted through Mr. Masovic. He gave extensive evidence on it. I don't think that's necessary right now. If we could go to 65 ter 24647. This is a report of an exhumation conducted in 1998 by the Sarajevo cantonal court of various sites in Rogatica, including Rasadnik. And if we could go to page 9 of the English and page 7 of the B/C/S, the first name under heading K, which is the Rasadnik site, is Hanka Kustura, the person whose name we just saw in the previous report, although according to this document she would have been 99 in 1994 and not 101. It appears to be the same person. If we could go to the next page in the English, page 8 in the B/C/S, another body exhumed is that of Aisa Osmanovic who would have been 95 years old at the time of the war who had been residing in Citici [phoen]. The next name is Halil Vatres who would have been in his mid-60s who had been residing in Rogatica. If we could go to the next page in both languages, number 16, Ibrahim Karaman. Sefik Hurko testified that a person by the name of Ibro Karaman was killed in December 1992 at Rasadnik. He would have been 76 at the time. The next page in the English and B/C/S number 18, Himzo Brankovic, another person that Sefik Hurko testified was killed in December 1992 in Rasadnik. He would have been 62. And if we could go to number 20, which is the next page in the English and same page in the B/C/S, Hajra Hodzic, a woman who would have been in her 70s who had been living in Kovanja. And the next page in both languages we have a couple, Sema and Bajro Colic, who would have been in their 60s, from Kovanja. All these bodies were exhumed at Rasadnik, several of whom we know from other evidence were detained at Rasadnik and/or killed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's clear, is it not, Mr. Lelek, that ordinary civilians were being detained at Rasadnik and indeed some of them met their end there?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: There was civilians detained when the high school centre was closed, but it doesn't make sense for somebody to kill a 101-year-old elderly woman as it appears from this document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the rest of the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please ask the witness to speak slower because it's not registered that he said: I had already told that there were civilians there. A lot is lost from the transcript, although I wanted to ask my colleague, Ms. Gustafson, where does it say that they were killed? If it says that they died, it does not necessarily mean that they were killed. And I'm afraid that this is misleading the witness. The witness is being misdirected.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just to clarify, I didn't say that that's what this document said. I said that there was other evidence that some of these people were killed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But shall we ask the witness to repeat what he said at the end of his answer? Did you say something else after having said, "... it doesn't make sense for someone to kill a 101-year-old elderly woman as it appears from this document"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I don't see any reason for killing old women of 80 or of 90 or for killing civilians at all. I don't know if all of that was at Rasadnik. How do I know? Perhaps they were buried in some Muslim village and then later it was said that the body was exhumed in Rasadnik. I don't believe what it says on the face of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, if I may, precisely what you asked is the result of the misleading. The witness was told that it is written in the document that they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On what grounds, may we please be told?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: On the grounds that this witness asserted that Rasadnik was a military detention facility and I don't think the Defence has any concerns about the authenticity of this record. If they do, I'm sure they'll inform the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness hasn't confirmed anything about the document, so I don't believe it can be admitted through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Mr. Robinson. Unless it is contradictory to what he said, I think it's difficult to admit this document through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I should have been clearer. That's what I meant when I said that the witness said that this -- that Rasadnik was a military detention facility. This document contradicts the witness. It shows that there were people who only could have been civilians at the time who were exhumed at the Rasadnik site, and the other evidence in this case connects these names or a number of these names to people who were detained at Rasadnik and indeed killed there. So certainly together with other evidence in this case it contradicts what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At the moment the Chamber has not been presented with the evidence which links this report to those who were detained in that detention unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: One of the documents was the first document I showed to the witness which was the exchange report -- reporting that Hanka Kustura had died at Rasadnik prison. She's one of the names in this. And Sefik Hurko testified at 18235 and 18236 that Ibro Karaman and Himzo Brankovic were killed at Rasadnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think I saw only Hanka Kustura's name in the previous report.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, and then -- but Sefik Hurko testified about three other names in this report: Ibrahim Karaman, Himzo Brankovic, and Becir Catahija [phoen]. He gave evidence that all of those people were killed while detained at Rasadnik. And that's at transcript 18235 to 18236 and P3267, paragraph 38.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having heard this, would you like to add anything, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think those facts are already in the record without the admission of the document, so I don't think it's necessary to admit the document. It doesn't add anything to the evidence and they can argue from what has already been testified to that certain portions of this document are inconsistent with the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are satisfied with your explanation as regards the contradiction. The Chamber will receive those pages shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, again I would just seek this clarification. The Prosecutor said that it was being tendered on the basis of the fact that the witness said that it was just for military personnel. The witness said only that after the school was closed there were civilians there. So it's incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, well, after I showed him the document he did say that, but that's not a reason to exclude the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. The Chamber has explained its reason for admitting this. Let's proceed. Let's give the number first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6152, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, you mentioned the village of Berkovici a few times. It was earlier in your evidence you said it was one of the loyal villages where the Serb authorities had a good relationship with the inhabitants, but then just a few moments ago you explained that there were some people from Berkovici detained at Rasadnik. Can you reconcile those two claims, on the one hand these villagers were loyal and on the other hand some of them were detained at Rasadnik?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I said already three or four times that in Rasadnik it was -- this was a military detention and the collection centre was in the high school. When the high school closed, that collection centre was transferred to Rasadnik and it was next to the facility where the military detention was so that in Rasadnik there was the same collection centre as there -- as the one in the high school. When the high school one closed, then the Muslims from Berkovici and Bucani were then received in Rasadnik in August. And you can see that people from Berkovici were brought to the collection centre in November. How could they have been taken to the high school when the high school was closed? We took them to the reception centre or they were taken to the reception centre in Rasadnik, which was next to the military detention. So they were not brought to the military detention centre but to the collection centre there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And how long were these civilians detained at Rasadnik?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if it's the interpretation that's incorrect. How can they be detained when the man said that they were not detained?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I don't see that anywhere.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said that they were brought to the reception centre, next building to the detention.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, is it your evidence that these civilians were detained at Rasadnik or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: These people were not detained in Rasadnik. They were in the collection centre, in the reception centre because they didn't have any reception centre after August except the one in Rasadnik. And you can see by the date that the high school was closed in August and that they were brought there in November.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 24478, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, this is a Drina Corps report from April 1993 and it's titled: List of captured persons of Muslim ethnicity in Rogatica, Visegrad, Rudo, Cajnice, and Foca. If we go to numbers 14, 15, and 16, you can see that there are three female Muslim names - Fata Kepes, Fatima Kepes, and Esma Kepes - women from Berkovici, one of who was 80 years old. And on the next page in the English number 24 and 25 two males from Berkovici, one of who would have been 14. And another name from Berkovici is at number 36. These people are being referred to as captured persons of Muslim ethnicity. They were prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: No, that is not right. They were placed in the reception centre in Rasadnik because the high school was closed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First let us establish whether this is Rasadnik here. Secondly, were they captured in Berkovici or are these some people who were at the front and not in Berkovici? There's confusion, total confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If the accused wants to ask further questions on redirect, he can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6153, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, I just have one last area to cover with you. At paragraph 24 of your statement you said: "I know that captured personnel of the Muslim army from Zepa and Srebrenica were not brought to Rogatica." Now, that is stated in categorical terms, so I take it that if Muslim prisoners had been brought to Rogatica from Zepa or Srebrenica that is something that you would have been aware of, being the Chief of Staff at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I did not say that. I said that I did not see anyone from Zepa being brought to Rasadnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So would you like to change your evidence, whereas before you said categorically: I know that captured personnel from the Muslim army from Zepa and Srebrenica were not brought to Rogatica. Is it your evidence now that that's not something that you know for sure, it's just that you didn't see anyone from Zepa being brought to Rasadnik?
