utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: May I just read this for a moment, please. I said here that I was aware that Muslim soldiers from Zepa and Srebrenica were not brought to Rogatica nor were they detained in the Agrokombinat and Sumarstvo facilities. Is that what you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm asking you whether it is your evidence that you categorically know that no captured personnel from Zepa or Srebrenica were brought to Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I state with full responsibility that the -- they were not brought to the Sumarstvo and the other facilities because they're in a populated place. There is a building there where two families lived throughout the whole war --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I wasn't talking specifically about those locations. I was talking about anywhere in Rogatica. I take it that you actually don't know whether or not Zepa prisoners were brought to Rasadnik. That's something you don't know one way or another; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I don't know that they were brought. Had they been brought in by force, I would have known but I didn't see that so I assert that they were not brought there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd just like to ask you one last question and that's from 65 ter 24651. I'd just like to read to you an extract from a statement you gave to the Prosecution in 2011. It was quite recent so I'm sure you recall giving that statement. And the passage I'd like to read to you is at page 33 of the English and page 49 of the B/C/S. And this is in connection with your evidence earlier today that there was no intimidation of the Muslim population. So this is from the very end of your interview where you say you'd just like to add a few sentences. And about halfway down the large passage at the bottom of the page you're talking about March or April 1992 when you were at your village with your parents you said: "When it was obvious from the media that the war was inevitable I put their children in a car," and you're talking about the children of a Muslim colleague from the TO, "I took them down to Rogatica although I came upon Serb barricade and I had to hide the children because I was afraid for their security and my colleague and his wife went on foot to Rogatica, on shortcut. We all met in Rogatica, I gave him the children; we sat in a bar that was just down here. We had five or six drinks maybe, said good-bye, and departed. I wanted to say that I wasn't for this but I had to be part of ... and I had to be with my people." Now, first, I'd just like to ask you, this is accurate? This happened the way you said, the way you told the Prosecution it happened?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I said that that's how it happened. May I be allowed to clarify. I went to Dobromirovici to see my parents, as I said. After a certain amount of time my friend came who used to work with me at the defence and he brought his wife and two children. And then he stayed with me in the village. And then through the media when it was evident that war was coming, I advised them and they said themselves, "Milovan, we have to separate. You have to go with your people. We have to go with our people." And he went on foot from my village to Rogatica, some 4 or 5 kilometres away. The children were small. I put his children in my car and I took them to Rogatica via Seljani. There was a Serb barricade. On the halfway point from Seljani to Rogatica it was in a Serb village. It wasn't even a barricade. I mean, people were standing on the road, they put some blockage across the road and I took the children safely to Rogatica. I handed them over to his parents. We sat down. We had a few drinks. We exchanged. We embraced each other and took our leave, and that's what happened. And I said then that I was not in favour of war, but when I saw that war was inevitable it's a normal thing that I would stand by my people and he would stand by his.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Just one question. You said you hid the children at the barricade because you were afraid for their security. Is the reason that the parents of the children didn't come with you in the car and they went on foot, is that because you didn't consider it safe for them to be travelling with you in your car?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I don't know that I said that I concealed them. The children could not go on foot. These were small children. They could not go on foot with their parents. I put them in my car and I drove them to Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions. I'd just like to tender this page of the witness's interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, there's nothing inconsistent in the page. The witness said that's how it happened so I don't believe there is any need to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I thought so too until his last answer when he said, I don't know that I concealed them, when he said that he had to hide the children because he was afraid for their security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6154, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. We'll begin with the latest point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This page from a document was shown to you, Mr. Lelek, regarding your assertion that Muslims had not been intimidated and it has to do with that claim that there was shooting around Muslim villages to intimidate them. Tell me, what intimidated this colleague of yours so that he came to stay with you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. President, who scared him. He was afraid of the situation in Rogatica because by that time there was talk already about the division of the MUP, of the Territorial Defence, of the Municipal Assembly, and since we were on good terms he saw me as a savior, so to speak, and he came to me to help him save his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What attitude did the authorities, the Serb authorities, take towards the intimidation of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Nobody intimidated anybody. Until that event of the 22nd of May, it was quiet until then. There was no conflict. It's true that tensions rose all the time, listening to all sorts of media. And as soon as talks started about division it was clear that it was not good. Until then we had lived shoulder to shoulder, Muslim and Serb neighbours. There had never been any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On pages 82 and 83 you were asked about investigations against Muslims in Rasadnik. Can you tell me, first of all, what is the difference between those who were placed in the secondary school centre and those who were placed in the detention unit in Rasadnik?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Those placed in the secondary school were Muslims who had not displayed any extremism. The others who were placed in the remand prison had weapons on them and they were suspect in some way. They had fired at Serb villages or something like that, and the former group never displayed any extremism against the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your evidence you said that you visited some of your own soldiers in Rasadnik. Tell me about all the people who were detained in Rasadnik.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Those who deserted from the lines, those who drank excessively. We were there to conduct interviews with them. There were several of them. You know there has to be discipline in the army. You know how troops have to behave in keeping with the rules of the service that applied before the war and that we --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last part of the answer. The witness has to be asked to speak more slowly and distinctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I should ask you again to speak very slowly and distinctly. The interpreters missed the last part of your answer with regards to rules of service. Could you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We detained our own soldiers there, those who deserted from the front line or drank in excess or were responsible for any other violation of discipline. We brought them to the remand prison. We interrogated them there before returning them to their units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked on page 68 whether any Serb soldier had been punished for any act committed against a Muslim. I am asking you, though, whether it was established that a soldier was responsible for a criminal offence and that was then covered up.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: We had no information that any soldier was guilty of a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a reserve officer and the assistant commander of the Territorial Defence before the war, were you familiar with the provisions of the Law on All People's Defence and social self-protection, especially as far as civilians in combat zones are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I was aware of those provisions. I and all the commanding officers of all units, whenever we came to the front line and whenever commands were given, those commands included caution that we have to treat civilians in keeping with the Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 81 a quotation was given to you, namely, that due to the attack on Seljani everybody had to go to the high school centre. Can you tell us, is it the duty of the army to evacuate people from a village about to be attacked?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I did not understand you, Mr. President. Can you repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were -- was the village of Seljani attacked? Because it was said that due to the attack on Seljani that was about to start they had to go to the high school centre?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Seljani village was not attacked. It was a majority Serb village with only a few Muslim houses. It was not possible for us to shell that village, and that village was never shelled nor threatened. There were just a few Muslim houses all the rest was Serb population. There was never an attack on Seljani village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In villages that were threatened by an attack, what did you do with their Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: We placed them in collection centres for their own safety. If they were threatened by Muslims from Oskoplje, Berkovici and Gucevo, we took them to collection centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at 65 ter 7272. I'm not sure we have a translation. Please look at this. On 12 June there's this regular combat report and the first sentence reads: "In the area of the municipality the enemy manifested itself in several places, infiltrating sabotage terrorist groups ..." et cetera. Further below it says: "In the town a large concentration of Muslim population is noted. They are moving into the high school centre. Most of them are women and children and there are also unarmed men. Around the town also visible are snipers who fired on the town as a motorcade, a convoy of vehicles, was passing through the town going towards Gorazde." First of all, how does this relate to your awareness of the presence of this -- of these civilians in the high school centre? Does it follow that they were brought there by force?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: They were not brought by force. Those were Muslim people who stayed behind in the town. And we called upon the Muslim population that was loyal, expressed its loyalty, and was not willing to fight to move to the high school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What kind of convoy was it that it was moving through the town towards Gorazde and subjected to sniping?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: According to the statement of Meho Alagic there were about 120 remaining armed Muslims and later he brought another 80 armed fighters. That's confirmed by the fact that when Pribosevic [phoen] village was attacked two of our men who were village guards were killed and then later a group of armed men from Rogatica moved towards Kupljace [phoen]. And we all know about the massacre committed against the population from Gorazde that was supposed to come to Rogatica. We know that in the area of Kukavice 25 civilians were ambushed and killed, 80 were wounded, and in that convoy there were about 1.000 civilians. Only thanks to the rapid intervention of our brigade were these civilians liberated from encirclement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It says here that a convoy of vehicles was going through -- towards the town and some towards Gorazde. How were these two columns moving and how did the Muslim snipers fire at them?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: It's certain that they wanted as much population to stay in town as possible because they didn't want to surrender the town. They wanted to fight. They wanted to keep the town in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But we don't understand, who was going towards Gorazde, Serbs or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Only Muslims because Serbs had no way of going towards Gorazde, no reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will leave this subject. This interview in 2004, how long was it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted, Your Excellencies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3035, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A note from that interview was shown to you; that's 65 ter 6151. How long was your interview with police of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Which one? With which interview? I can't see anything on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness P6151.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's clear only now. You don't have to show it now. I remember. That interview was just 10, 15 minutes, not longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read and sign this?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I don't think I signed this. I know they talked to me, but there is no indication that I signed it here. And it didn't even take part on the official premises of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Earlier today you heard a quotation from Mr. Ujic that was on page 33460. The quotation was incomplete. I'll read now to you in English that quotation so it can be more accurately interpreted: [In English] "Q. Now, Mr. Ujic, is it your position that the Rogatica Territorial Defence, Rogatica Brigade never -- whatever you want to call it, shelled five Muslim villages and part of the town and carried out an infantry attack all in order to create a corridor to move -- to remove the body of the killed Serb. Is that your position?" [Interpretation] And the answer: [In English] "A. No, I need to explain that. The aforementioned villages of Pokrivenik and others, Cadovi and others, parts of Kozici and Cadovina were mixed, although there were more Muslims than Serbs there. The village of Trnovo is in the area too where the Serbs were 100 per cent of the population. On the other hand, there was the village of Pokrivenik which was 100 per cent Muslims. From such villages there were attacks on the other villages where there were many civilian casualties. For example, the Obradovic family from Trnovo was killed, all of them, the husband, wife, and underaged daughter who had also been raped. And in order to extract their body we had to engage and neutralise the fire coming from such villages that was directed to us. " [Interpretation] And further below it says -- I won't read everything. Witness Ujic says on the previous page 33460: [In English] "We opened fire on the enemy strongholds of Dub, Pokrivenik, Kopljevici, Kozeici, Cadovi, as well as on Pasic Kula, Rajs Laze and Rudo 2 settlement. In the town an infantry attack was carried out on the area of Rajs Laze and Rudo." [Interpretation] And you told us here that there was an infantry in town. You said the attack on Rajs Laze and Rudo 2?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it sound more complete and clearer now what Mr. Ujic said and was it true what he said, that those were strongholds and you were exposed to fire from them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The part you read out in the last -- at the end is a part of question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, also, Your Honour, the only evidence of Mr. Ujic that I put to this witness was in relation to this witness's claim that there was no shelling on the 22nd of May, and I put to him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm going to read out the relevant part. That's the summary of the document after reading out that part the Prosecutor asked this question: "Now, this reference to opening fire on these locations, that's a reference to a shelling attack; right?" Answer, Mr. Ujic: "Well, shelling as well as an infantry attack. It was a combined operation." That's the evidence we received.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this, Your Excellency, is a question that quotes from a Serb document that Mr. Ujic was confronted with and it follows from it that there was no shelling in town. There was an infantry attack. However, there was artillery fire opened on villages that were strongholds and that's what this witness said, that there was fire from anti-aircraft guns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, the witness said various things. Now Mr. Karadzic is providing his own interpretation to a document that's not been shown to the witness. It's just -- this is just confusing and I don't think it's getting us anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is: Was Rogatica shelled on 22nd May, as the Prosecution suggests?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I was asked about that by the Prosecution, I think, and I said that after -- on 22nd May Rogatica was not shelled because at that time there was both Serb and Muslim population in town. There was one part of the road from Rudo towards Zlatni Do, where there was a stronghold of Muslims up to Laze, where the body of late Mihajlovic was. We could not pull that body out without using the anti-aircraft gun only in a limited area around the road only to prepare the terrain for pulling out the body. We couldn't shell the town, of course, because there were Serbs and Muslims there still. We couldn't shell our own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lelek, I will read to you from P3265, it's a combat report of 23rd May, a day later. It says: "Above the Serbian municipality of Rogatica on 22nd May we opened fire at the enemy stronghold Dub, Kopljevici, Kozici as well as Pasina Kula and Rudo 2. In Rajs Laze and Rudo 2 there was an infantry attack, the enemy was crushed and suffered losses." Is this report accurate and does it make a distinction between the town and these strongholds?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes, it does. And I repeat, we didn't shell the town. We shelled above Rudo 2, that's when you exit Rogatica to go to Zlatni Do. That's to say we only used the anti-aircraft gun along the roads so as to be able to go to Zlatni Do and pull out the body of the late Mihajlovic. We did not open fire on Rudo, which I consider a part of the town although there were no houses there. There's a meadow. There is a clearing next to the road 15, 20 metres from the road. We fired only there to be able to get in and get the body out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 7220 of the 24th of June. Regular combat report of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you speak of this attempt to get the body out and so on and so forth, was there any fighting going on or was this a one-sided activity by you? Did you come up against any kind of resistance? Well, this question has nothing to do with the document whatsoever, sir. Was there any fighting there or was this one-sided from your side?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Had there not been fighting, we wouldn't have used the anti-aircraft gun, Mr. President, had we been able to get in and get the body out. So from Rudo to Zlatni Do to where the body was, the body of the late Mihajlovic because Zlatni Do was a major stronghold. There were lots of enemy forces there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please take a look at this, this report of the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. So let us disregard this Sovrle and then it says: "In the area of Kramer Selo, Golubovici, Vragolovi and Gornja Kukavica, enemy forces have been observed to be concentrating. The commander of the Rogatica Brigade said that enemy losses in the course of yesterday's battles amount to ten enemy soldiers killed and one captured." Are you familiar with this period and is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I can't see these villages here. What are the villages?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Kramer Selo, Golubovici, Vragolovi, and Gornja Kukavica.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes, the area of Vragolovi, that's where the enemy was, major enemy concentrations in the area of Vragolovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3036, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just one more document. Can we please call up 65 ter 7791.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we see the signature. Did somebody sign on Rajko Kusic's behalf? It looks like that. Could we have the first page, please. The first page, please. This is a report of the Rogatica Brigade for the 9th of June, 1992. And now these two lines. It says here: "In town there was noticeable activity in the return of the enemy to town. Snipers are active on several locations in town." Does this correspond to your knowledge, that they returned to town, that their fighters returned to the town of Rogatica, that is?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: It does correspond to that because for a while they were deployed in Ljun, this is a hill above town, and then Zivaljevina is over there, it's a Serb village, but then there is more of the hill of Ljun behind that village. And that's probably where they sought shelter in basements, or rather, in basements in town or some shelters or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It says here in the last paragraph towards the bottom it says: "Parts of the brigade are engaged in town in combat with the enemy who is retreating into town. There were no casualties on our side, one soldier was wounded in town while the enemy has 20 dead and several wounded soldiers." Can you explain this to us, what does this mean that the enemy is withdrawing into town?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Well, they tried to attack our villages and then the outskirts of town too, the neighbourhood of Karanfil and Donje Polje. And when fire was opened at them then they withdrew due to the losses they had. They withdrew into town and sought shelter in safe locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question in relation to that list of persons where it says persons who were taken prisoner from Berkovici, that was the question, 6153, that's it. P6153. Now, does that indicate that these people were in Rasadnik and that they died in Rasadnik and that they had been staying in Rasadnik? Did you notice that? Actually, let's call up the document. Let's have the document and you take a look at it. 6152 -- or no, 53, yes, that's right. Now let us zoom in and let us see what is written there exactly. It says here persons of Muslim ethnicity from the areas of Rogatica, Visegrad, Rudo, Cajnice, and Foca.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it say anywhere where these people were put up?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: No, it just says list of captured persons of Muslim ethnicity in the areas of Rogatica, Visegrad, Rudo, Cajnice, and Foca. It doesn't say anywhere that they were put up at Rasadnik. No, no, it's not written anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this group of captured persons?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I don't know anything. Most probably it was at the municipality then because it was the municipality that made lists of civilian and persons who were taken prisoner, and then they were taken further on to the places where they wanted to go or where they would be staying. Now I know that in Rasadnik at the time there were some villagers from Berkovici and Gucevo but I don't know whether it was these persons because I had no contact with them. I had not seen them. I quite simply --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, again the witness -- the interpreter didn't hear the witness. He spoke too fast. What did you say, Mr. Lelek, after asking said "I had not seen them"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that from this list I cannot conclude whether these persons were at Rasadnik or not. I did not see them. Only the lists could be checked of persons -- I mean, the lists that the civilian authorities of the municipality had because they kept lists of the Muslim population that was at the collection centres and that were taken there to where they wanted to go in order to change their place of residence. I don't know about these persons. And then I said I saw Sahin Suceska from Berkovici and Kustur [phoen]. By sight I cannot remember the first names now, but I did know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did all the villagers of Berkovici stay on in Berkovici, or could somebody have been in a Muslim unit outside Berkovici? Did that happen? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Well, Berkovici and Oskoplje are two neighbouring villages and it's certain that there were extremists from Berkovici that joined those in Oskoplje, and that is why they threatened the local population of Berkovici, that they would kill them because they were co-operating with the Serbs. It is certain that there were persons from Berkovici who left Berkovici and joined some other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last question: Did you know whether in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina there were any women?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I didn't know that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this previous document, 7791?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3037, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellencies. No further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lelek, now that concludes your evidence. Thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll rise all together. We'll resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
